entries.29aea8fac431895d83221a38f044f6f15f13dafb: <div sID="gen31171" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="9" osisID="1Cor.9" sID="1Cor.9"/> <div eID="gen31171" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31172" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen31173" type="x-p"/> In this chapter the apostle seems to answer some cavils against himself. I. He asserts his apostolical mission and authority, and gives in his success among them as a testimony to it, <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.1-1Cor.9.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>. II. He claims a right to subsist by his ministry, and defends it by several arguments from natural reason and the Mosaical law, and asserts it also to be a constitution of Christ, <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.3-1Cor.9.14">ver. 3-14</reference>. III. He shows that he had willingly waived this privilege and power for their benefit, <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.15-1Cor.9.18">ver. 15-18</reference>. IV. He specifies several other things, in which he had denied himself for the sake of other men's spiritual interest and salvation, <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.19-1Cor.9.23">ver. 19-23</reference>. And, V. Concludes his argument by showing what animated him to this course, even the prospect of an incorruptible crown, <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.24-1Cor.9.27">ver. 24, to the end</reference>.
entries.d7088d6f0d52083ca1909f622246e407c0140047: <div eID="gen31173" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen31172" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Rights of a Christian Minister. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 57.)</title> <div sID="gen31174" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Am I not an apostle? am I not free? have I not seen Jesus Christ our Lord? are not ye my work in the Lord? <hi type="super">2</hi> If I be not an apostle unto others, yet doubtless I am to you: for the seal of mine apostleship are ye in the Lord. <div eID="gen31174" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31175" type="x-p"/> Blessed Paul, in the work of his ministry, not only met with opposition from those without, but discouragement from those within. He was under reproach; false brethren questioned his apostleship, and were very industrious to lessen his character and sink his reputation; particularly here at Corinth, a place to which he had been instrumental in doing much good, and from which he had deserved well; and yet there were those among them who upon these heads created him great uneasiness. Note, It is no strange nor new thing for a minister to meet with very unkind returns for great good-will to a people, and diligent and successful services among them. Some among the Corinthians questioned, if they did not disown, his apostolical character. To their cavils he here answers, and in such a manner as to set forth himself as a remarkable example of that self-denial, for the good of others, which he had been recommending in the former chapter. And, 1. He asserts his apostolical mission and character: <hi type="italic">Am I not an apostle? Have I not seen Jesus Christ our Lord?</hi> To be a witness of his resurrection was one great branch of the apostolical charge. "Now," says Paul, "have not I seen the Lord, though not immediately after his resurrection, yet since his ascent?" See <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.8">ch. iv. 8</reference>. "<hi type="italic">Am I not free?</hi> Have I not the same commission, and charge, and powers, with the other apostles? What respect, or honour, or subsistence, can they challenge, which I am not at liberty to demand as well as they?" It was not because he had no right to live of the gospel that he maintained himself with his own hands, but for other reasons. 2. He offers the success of his ministry among them, and the good he had done to them, as a proof of his apostleship: "<hi type="italic">Are not you my work in the Lord?</hi> Through the blessing of Christ on my labours, have not I raised a church among you? <hi type="italic">The seal of my apostleship are you in the Lord.</hi> Your conversion by my means is a confirmation from God of my mission." Note, The ministers of Christ should not think it strange to be put upon the proof of their ministry by some who have had experimental evidence of the power of it and the presence of God with it. 3. He justly upbraids the Corinthians with their disrespect: "<hi type="italic">Doubtless, if I am not an apostle to others, I am so to you,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.2">v. 2</reference>. I have laboured so long, and with so much success, among you, that you, above all others, should own and honour my character, and not call it in question." Note, It is no new thing for faithful ministers to meet with the worst treatment where they might expect the best. This church at Corinth had as much reason to believe, and as little reason to question, his apostolical mission, as any; they had as much reason, perhaps more than any church, to pay him respect. He had been instrumental in bringing them to the knowledge and faith of Christ; he laboured long among them, nearly two years, and he laboured to good purpose, <hi type="italic">God having much people among them.</hi> See <reference osisRef="Acts.18.10-Acts.18.11">Acts xviii. 10, 11</reference>. It was aggravated ingratitude for this people to call in question his authority.
entries.0c8cd9d8a01961c4a6ecd81e43071a8776adcb92: <div eID="gen31175" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Rights of a Christian Minister. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 57.)</title> <div sID="gen31176" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">3</hi> Mine answer to them that do examine me is this, <hi type="super">4</hi> Have we not power to eat and to drink? <hi type="super">5</hi> Have we not power to lead about a sister, a wife, as well as other apostles, and <hi type="italic">as</hi> the brethren of the Lord, and Cephas? 6 Or I only and Barnabas, have not we power to forbear working? <hi type="super">7</hi> Who goeth a warfare any time at his own charges? who planteth a vineyard, and eateth not of the fruit thereof? or who feedeth a flock, and eateth not of the milk of the flock? 8 Say I these things as a man? or saith not the law the same also? <hi type="super">9</hi> For it is written in the law of Moses, Thou shalt not muzzle the mouth of the ox that treadeth out the corn. Doth God take care for oxen? <hi type="super">10</hi> Or saith he <hi type="italic">it</hi> altogether for our sakes? For our sakes, no doubt, <hi type="italic">this</hi> is written: that he that ploweth should plow in hope; and that he that thresheth in hope should be partaker of his hope. <hi type="super">11</hi> If we have sown unto you spiritual things, <hi type="italic">is it</hi> a great thing if we shall reap your carnal things? <hi type="super">12</hi> If others be partakers of <hi type="italic">this</hi> power over you, <hi type="italic">are</hi> not we rather? Nevertheless we have not used this power; but suffer all things, lest we should hinder the gospel of Christ. <hi type="super">13</hi> Do ye not know that they which minister about holy things live <hi type="italic">of the things</hi> of the temple? and they which wait at the altar are partakers with the altar? <hi type="super">14</hi> Even so hath the Lord ordained that they which preach the gospel should live of the gospel. <div eID="gen31176" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31177" type="x-p"/> Having asserted his apostolical authority, he proceeds to claim the rights belonging to his office, especially that of being maintained by it. <div eID="gen31177" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31178" type="x-p"/> I. These he states, <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.3-1Cor.9.6">v. 3-6</reference>. "<hi type="italic">My answer to those that do examine me</hi> (that is, enquire into my authority, or the reasons of my conduct, if I am an apostle) is this: <hi type="italic">Have we not power to eat and drink</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.9.4">v. 4</reference>), or a right to maintenance? <hi type="italic">Have we not power to lead about a sister, a wife, as well as other apostles, and the brethren of the Lord, and Cephas;</hi> and, not only to be maintained ourselves, but have them maintained also?" Though Paul was at that time single, he had a right to take a wife when he pleased, and to lead her about with him, and expect a maintenance for her, as well as himself, from the churches. Perhaps Barnabas had a wife, as the other apostles certainly had, and led them about with them. For that a wife is here to be understood by the <hi type="italic">sister-woman</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">adelphen gynaika,</hi></hi> is plain from this, that it would have been utterly unfit for the apostles to have carried about women with them unless they were wives. The word implies that they had power over them, and could require their attendance on them, which none could have over any but wives or servants. Now the apostles, who worked for their bread, do not seem to have been in a capacity to buy or have servants to carry with them. Not to observe that it would have raised suspicion to have carried about even women-servants, and much more other women to whom they were not married, for which the apostles would never give any occasion. The apostle therefore plainly asserts he had a right to marry as well as other apostles, and claim a maintenance for his wife, nay, and his children too, if he had any, from the churches, without labouring with his own hands to procure it. <hi type="italic">Or I only and Barnabas, have not we power to for bear working?</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.6">v. 6</reference>. In short, the apostle here claims a maintenance from the churches, both for him and his. This was due from them, and what he might claim. <div eID="gen31178" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31179" type="x-p"/> II. He proceeds, by several arguments, to prove his claim. 1. From the common practice and expectations of mankind. Those who addict and give themselves up to any way of business in the world expect to live out of it. Soldiers expect to be paid for their service. Husbandmen and shepherds expect to get a livelihood out of their labours. If they plant vineyards, and dress and cultivate them, it is with expectation of fruit; if they feed a flock, it is with the expectation of being fed and clothed by it! <hi type="italic">Who goeth a warfare at any time at his own charge? Who planteth a vineyard, and eateth not the fruit thereof? Who feedeth a flock, and eateth not the milk thereof?</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.7-1Cor.9.9">v. 7-9</reference>. Note, It is very natural, and very reasonable, for ministers to expect a livelihood out of their labours. 2. He argues it out of the Jewish law: <hi type="italic">Say I these things as a man? Or saith not the law the same also?</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.8">v. 8</reference>. Is this merely a dictate of common reason and according to common usage only? No, it is also consonant to the old law. God had therein ordered that the ox should not be muzzled while he was treading out the corn, nor hindered from eating while he was preparing the corn for man's use, and treading it out of the ear. But this law was not chiefly given out of God's regard to oxen, or concern for them, but to teach mankind that all due encouragement should be given to those who are employed by us, or labouring for our good—that the labourers should taste of the fruit of their labours. <hi type="italic">Those who plough should plough in hope; and those who thresh in hope should be partakers of their hope,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.10">v. 10</reference>. The law saith this about oxen for our sakes. Note, Those that lay themselves out to do our souls good should not have their mouths muzzled, but have food provided for them. 3. He argues from common equity: <hi type="italic">If we have sown unto you spiritual things, is it a great thing if we shall reap your carnal things?</hi> What they had sown was much better than they expected to reap. They had taught them the way to eternal life, and laboured heartily to put them in possession of it. It was no great matter, surely, while they were giving themselves up to this work, to expect a support of their own temporal life. They had been instruments of conveying to them the greater spiritual blessings; and had they no claim to as great a share in their carnal things as was necessary to subsist them? Note, Those who enjoy spiritual benefits by the ministry of the word should not grudge a maintenance to such as are employed in this work. If they have received a real benefit, one would think they could not grudge them this. What, get so much good by them, and yet grudge to do so little good to them! Is this grateful or equitable? 4. He argues from the maintenance they afforded others: "<hi type="italic">If others are partakers of this power over you, are not we rather?</hi> You allow others this maintenance, and confess their claim just; but who has so just a claim as I from the church of Corinth? Who has given greater evidence of the apostolic mission? Who had laboured so much for your good, or done like service among you?" Note, Ministers should be valued and provided for according to their worth. "<hi type="italic">Nevertheless,</hi>" says the apostle, "<hi type="italic">we have not used this power; but suffer all things, lest we should hinder the gospel of Christ.</hi> We have not insisted on our right, but have rather been in straits to serve the interests of the gospel, and promote the salvation of souls." He renounced his right, rather than by claiming it he would hinder his success. He denied himself, for fear of giving offence; but asserted his right lest his self-denial should prove prejudicial to the ministry. Note, He is likely to plead most effectually for the rights of others who shows a generous disregard to his own. It is plain, in this case, that justice, and not self-love, is the principle by which he is actuated. 5. He argues from the old Jewish establishment: "<hi type="italic">Do you not know that those who minister about holy things live of the things of the temple, and those who wait at the altar are partakers with the altar?</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.13">v. 13</reference>. And, if the Jewish priesthood was maintained out of the holy things that were then offered, shall not Christ's ministers have a maintenance out of their ministry? Is there not as much reason that we should be maintained as they?" He asserts it to be the institution of Christ: "<hi type="italic">Even so hath the Lord ordained that those who preach the gospel should live of the gospel</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.9.14">v. 14</reference>), should have a right to a maintenance, though not bound to demand it, and insist upon it." It is the people's duty to maintain their minister, by Christ's appointment, though it be not a duty bound on every minister to call for or accept it. He may waive his right, as Paul did, without being a sinner; but those transgress an appointment of Christ who deny or withhold it. Those who preach the gospel have a right to live by it; and those who attend on their ministry, and yet take no thought about their subsistence, fail very much in their duty to Christ, and respect owing to them.
entries.ab2e1e3339cfcdc088eab8d786492cb7124fdb58: <div eID="gen31179" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Apostle's Devotedness. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 57.)</title> <div sID="gen31180" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> But I have used none of these things: neither have I written these things, that it should be so done unto me: for <hi type="italic">it were</hi> better for me to die, than that any man should make my glorying void. <hi type="super">16</hi> For though I preach the gospel, I have nothing to glory of: for necessity is laid upon me; yea, woe is unto me, if I preach not the gospel! <hi type="super">17</hi> For if I do this thing willingly, I have a reward: but if against my will, a dispensation <hi type="italic">of the gospel</hi> is committed unto me. <hi type="super">18</hi> What is my reward then? <hi type="italic">Verily</hi> that, when I preach the gospel, I may make the gospel of Christ without charge, that I abuse not my power in the gospel. <div eID="gen31180" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31181" type="x-p"/> Here he tells them that he had, notwithstanding, waived his privilege, and lays down his reason for doing it. <div eID="gen31181" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31182" type="x-p"/> I. He tells them that he had neglected to claim his right in times past: <hi type="italic">I have used none of these things,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.15">v. 15</reference>. He neither ate nor drank himself at their cost, nor led about a wife to be maintained by them, nor forbore working to maintain himself. From others he received a maintenance, but not from them, for some special reasons. Nor did he write this to make his claim now. Though he here asserts his right, yet he does not claim his due; but denies himself for their sakes, and the gospel. <div eID="gen31182" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31183" type="x-p"/> II. We have the reason assigned of his exercising this self-denial. He would not have his glorying made void: <hi type="italic">It were better for his to die than that any man should make his glorying void,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.15">v. 15</reference>. This glorying did imply nothing in it of boasting, or self-conceit, or catching at applause, but a high degree of satisfaction and comfort. It was a singular pleasure to him to preach the gospel without making it burdensome; and he was resolved that among them he would not lose this satisfaction. His advantages for promoting the gospel were his glory, and he valued them above his rights, or his very life: <hi type="italic">Better were it for him to die than to have his glorying made void,</hi> than to have it justly said that he preferred his wages to his work. No, he was ready to deny himself for the sake of the gospel. Note, It is the glory of a minister to prefer the success of his ministry to his interest, and deny himself, that he may serve Christ, and save souls. Not that in so doing he does more than he ought; he is still acting within the bounds of the law of charity. But he acts upon truly noble principles, he brings much honour to God in so doing; and those that honour him he will honour. It is what God will approve and commend, what a man may value himself for and take comfort in, though he cannot make a merit of it before God. <div eID="gen31183" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31184" type="x-p"/> III. He shows that this self-denial was more honourable in itself, and yielded him much more content and comfort, than his preaching did: "<hi type="italic">Though I preach the gospel, I have nothing whereof to glory; for necessity is laid upon me; yea, woe is unto me, if I preach not the gospel,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.16">v. 16</reference>. It is my charge, my business; it is the work for which I am constituted an apostle, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.17">ch. i. 17</reference>. This is a duty expressly bound upon me. It is not in any degree a matter of liberty. <hi type="italic">Necessity is upon me.</hi> I am false and unfaithful to my trust, I break a plain and express command, and <hi type="italic">woe be to me, if I do not preach the gospel.</hi>" Those who are set apart to the office of the ministry have it in charge to preach the gospel. Woe be to them if they do not. From this none is excepted. But it is not given in charge to all, nor any preacher of the gospel, to do his work gratis, to preach and have no maintenance out of it. It is not said, "Woe be to him if he do not preach the gospel, and yet maintain himself." In this point he is more at liberty. It may be his duty to preach at some seasons, and under some circumstances, without receiving a maintenance for it; but he has, in the general, a right to it, and may expect it from those among whom he labours. When he renounces this right for the sake of the gospel and the souls of men, though he does not supererogate, yet he denies himself, waives his privilege and right; he does more than his charge and office in general, and at all times, obliges him to. Woe be to him if he do not preach the gospel; but it may sometimes be his duty to insist on his maintenance for so doing, and whenever he forbears to claim it he parts with his right, though a man may sometimes be bound to do so by the general duties of love to God and charity to men. Note, It is a high attainment in religion to renounce our own rights for the good of others; this will entitle to a peculiar reward from God. For, <div eID="gen31184" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31185" type="x-p"/> IV. The apostle here informs us that doing our duty with a willing mind will meet with a gracious recompence from God: <hi type="italic">If I do this thing,</hi> that is, either preach the gospel or take no maintenance, <hi type="italic">willingly, I have a reward.</hi> Indeed, it is willing service only that is capable of reward from God. It is not the bare doing of any duty, but the doing of it heartily (that is, willingly and cheerfully) that God has promised to reward. Leave the heart out of our duties, and God abhors them: they are but the carcasses, without the life and spirit, of religion. Those must preach willingly who would be accepted of God in this duty. They must make their business a pleasure, and not esteem it a drudgery. And those who, out of regard to the honour of God or good of souls, give up their claim to a maintenance, should do this duty willingly, if they would be accepted in it or rewarded for it. But whether the duty of the office be done willingly or with reluctance, whether the heart be in it or averse from it, all in office have a trust and charge from God, for which they must be accountable. Ministers have a dispensation of the gospel, or <hi type="italic">stewardship</hi>—<hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">oikonomia</hi></hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.16.2">Luke xvi. 2</reference>), committed to them. Note, Christ's willing servants shall not fail of a recompence, and that proportioned to their fidelity, zeal, and diligence; and his slothful and unwilling servants shall all be called to an account. Taking his name, and professing to do his business, will make men accountable at his bar. And how sad an account have slothful servants to give! <div eID="gen31185" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31186" type="x-p"/> V. The apostle sums up the argument, by laying before them the encouraging hope he had of a large recompence for his remarkable self-denial: <hi type="italic">What is my reward then?</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.18">v. 18</reference>. What is it I expect a recompence from God for? <hi type="italic">That when I preach the gospel I may make it without charge, that I abuse not my power in the gospel.</hi> Or, "not so to claim my rights as to make them destroy the great intentions and ends of my office, but renounce them for the sake of these." It is an abuse of power to employ it against the very ends for which it is given. And the apostle would never use his power, or privilege of being maintained by his ministry, so as to frustrate the ends of it, but would willingly and cheerfully deny himself for the honour of Christ and the interest of souls. That ministers who follows his example may have cheerful expectations of a full recompence.
entries.f9fdf1645e246a24bb436579390f37ad053cb023: <div eID="gen31186" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Apostle's Devotedness. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 57.)</title> <div sID="gen31187" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">19</hi> For though I be free from all <hi type="italic">men,</hi> yet have I made myself servant unto all, that I might gain the more. 20 And unto the Jews I became as a Jew, that I might gain the Jews; to them that are under the law, as under the law, that I might gain them that are under the law; <hi type="super">21</hi> To them that are without law, as without law, (being not without law to God, but under the law to Christ,) that I might gain them that are without law. <hi type="super">22</hi> To the weak became I as weak, that I might gain the weak: I am made all things to all <hi type="italic">men,</hi> that I might by all means save some. <hi type="super">23</hi> And this I do for the gospel's sake, that I might be partaker thereof with <hi type="italic">you.</hi> <div eID="gen31187" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31188" type="x-p"/> The apostle takes occasion from what he had before discoursed to mention some other instances of his self-denial and parting with his liberty for the benefit of others. <div eID="gen31188" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31189" type="x-p"/> I. He asserts his liberty (<reference osisRef="1Cor.9.19">v. 19</reference>): <hi type="italic">Though I be free from all men.</hi> He was free-born, a citizen of Rome. He was in bondage to none, nor depended upon any for his subsistence; <hi type="italic">yet he made himself a servant to all, that he might gain the more.</hi> He behaved as a servant; he laboured for their good as a servant; he was careful to please, as a servant to his master; he acted in many cases as if he had no privileges; and this that he might gain the more, or make the more converts to Christianity. He made himself a servant, that they might be made free. <div eID="gen31189" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31190" type="x-p"/> II. He specifies some particulars wherein he made himself a servant to all. He accommodated himself to all sorts of people. 1. <hi type="italic">To the Jews, and those under the law, he became a Jew,</hi> and as under the law, to gain them. Though he looked on the ceremonial law as a yoke taken off by Christ, yet in many instances he submitted to it, that he might work upon the Jews, remove their prejudices, prevail with them to hear the gospel, and win them over to Christ. 2. <hi type="italic">To those that are without the law as without law</hi> that is, to the Gentiles, whether converted to the Christian faith or not. In innocent things he could comply with people's usages or humours for their advantage. He would reason with the philosophers in their own way. And, as to converted Gentiles, he behaved among them as one that was not under the bondage of the Jewish laws, as he had asserted and maintained concerning them, though he did not act as a lawless person, but as one who was bound by the laws of Christ. He would transgress no laws of Christ to please or humour any man; but he would accommodate himself to all men, where he might do it lawfully, to gain some. Paul was the apostle of the Gentiles, and so, one would have thought, might have excused himself from complying with the Jews; and yet, to do them good, and win them over to Christ, he did, in innocent things, neglect the power he had to do otherwise, and conformed to some of their usages and laws. And though he might, by virtue of that character, have challenged authority over the Gentiles, yet he accommodated himself, as much as he innocently might, to their prejudices and ways of thinking. Doing good was the study and business of his life; and, so that he might reach this end, he did not stand on privileges and punctilios. 3. <hi type="italic">To the weak he became as weak, that he might gain the weak,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.22">v. 22</reference>. He was willing to make the best of them. He did not despise nor judge them, but became as one of them, forbore to use his liberty for their sake, and was careful to lay no stumbling-block in their way. Where any, through the weakness of their understanding, or the strength of their prejudices, were likely to fall into sin, or fall off from the gospel into heathen idolatry, through his use of his liberty, he refrained himself. He denied himself for their sakes, that he might insinuate into their affections, and gain their souls. In short, <hi type="italic">he became all things to all men, that he might by all means</hi> (all lawful means) <hi type="italic">gain some.</hi> He would not sin against God to save the soul of his neighbour, but he would very cheerfully and readily deny himself. The rights of God he could not give up, but he might resign his own, and he very often did so for the good of others. <div eID="gen31190" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31191" type="x-p"/> III. He assigns his reason for acting in this manner (<reference osisRef="1Cor.9.23">v. 23</reference>): <hi type="italic">This I do for the gospel's sake, and that I may be partaker thereof with you;</hi> that is, for the honour of Christ, whose the gospel is, and for the salvation of souls, for which it was designed, and that he and they might communicate in the privileges of it, or partake together of them. For these ends did he thus condescend, deny himself as to his liberty, and accommodate himself to the capacities and usages of those with whom he had to do, where he lawfully might. Note, A heart warmed with zeal for God, and breathing after the salvation of men, will not plead and insist upon rights and privileges in bar to this design. Those manifestly abuse their power in the gospel who employ it not to edification but destruction, and therefore breathe nothing of its spirit.
entries.1016e22a35c99dfaf5caff45e5fe4f800f30e14a: <div eID="gen31191" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Apostle's Devotedness. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 57.)</title> <div sID="gen31192" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">24</hi> Know ye not that they which run in a race run all, but one receiveth the prize? So run, that ye may obtain. 25 And every man that striveth for the mastery is temperate in all things. Now they <hi type="italic">do it</hi> to obtain a corruptible crown; but we an incorruptible. <hi type="super">26</hi> I therefore so run, not as uncertainly; so fight I, not as one that beateth the air: <hi type="super">27</hi> But I keep under my body, and bring <hi type="italic">it</hi> into subjection: lest that by any means, when I have preached to others, I myself should be a castaway. <div eID="gen31192" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31193" type="x-p"/> In these verses the apostle hints at the great encouragement he had to act in this manner. He had a glorious prize, an incorruptible crown, in view. Upon this head he compares himself to the racers and combatants in the Isthmian games, an allusion well known to the Corinthians, because they were celebrated in their neighbourhood: "<hi type="italic">Know you not that those who run in a race run all, but one obtaineth the prize?</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.24">v. 24</reference>. All run at your games, but only one gets the race and wins the crown." And here, <div eID="gen31193" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31194" type="x-p"/> I. He excites them to their duty: "<hi type="italic">So run that you may obtain.</hi> It is quite otherwise in the Christian race than in your races; only one wins the prize in them. You may all run so as to obtain. You have great encouragement, therefore, to persist constantly, and diligently, and vigorously, in your course. There is room for all to get the prize. You cannot fail if you run well. Yet there should be a noble emulation; you should endeavour to outdo one another. And it is a glorious contest who shall get first to heaven, or have the best rewards in that blessed world. I make it my endeavour to run; so do you, as you see me go before you." Note, It is the duty of Christians to follow their ministers closely in the chase of eternal glory, and the honour and duty of ministers to lead them in the way. <div eID="gen31194" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31195" type="x-p"/> II. He directs them in their course, by setting more fully to view his own example, still carrying on the allusion. 1. Those that ran in their games were kept to a set diet: "<hi type="italic">Every man that strives for the mastery is temperate in all things,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.23">v. 23</reference>. The fighters and wrestlers in your exercises are kept to strict diet and discipline; nay, they keep themselves to it. They do not indulge themselves, but restrain themselves from the food they eat and so from the liberties they use on other occasions. And should not Christians much more abridge themselves of their liberty, for so glorious an end as winning the race, and obtaining the prize set before them? They used a very spare diet, and course food, and denied themselves much, to prepare for their race and combat; so do I; so should you, after my example. It is hard if, for the heavenly crown, you cannot abstain from heathen sacrifices." 2. They were not only temperate, but inured themselves to hardships. Those who fought with one another in these exercises prepared themselves by beating the air, as the apostle calls it, or by throwing out their arms, and thereby inuring themselves, beforehand, to deal about their blows in close combat, or brandish them by way of flourish. There is no room for any such exercise in the Christian warfare. Christians are ever in close combat. There enemies make fierce and hearty opposition, and are ever at hand; and for this reason they must lay about them in earnest, and never drop the contest, nor flag and faint in it. They must fight, not as those that beat the air, but must strive against their enemies with all their might. One enemy the apostle here mentions, namely, the body; this must be kept under, beaten black and blue, as the combatants were in these Grecian games, and thereby brought into subjection. By the body we are to understand fleshly appetites and inclinations. These the apostle set himself to curb and conquer, and in this the Corinthians were bound to imitate him. Note, Those who would aright pursue the interests of their souls must beat down their bodies, and keep them under. They must combat hard with fleshly lusts, and not indulge a wanton appetite, and long for heathenish sacrifices, nor eat them, to please their flesh, at the hazard of their brethren's souls. The body must be made to serve the mind, not suffered to lord over it. <div eID="gen31195" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31196" type="x-p"/> III. The apostle presses this advice on the Corinthians by proper arguments drawn from the same contenders. 1. They take pains, and undergo all those hardships, <hi type="italic">to obtain a corruptible crown</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.9.25">v. 25</reference>), <hi type="italic">but we an incorruptible.</hi> Those who conquered in these games were crowned only with the withering leaves or boughs of trees, of olive, bays, or laurel. But Christians have an incorruptible crown in view, a crown of glory that never fadeth away, an inheritance incorruptible, reserved in heaven for them. And would they yet suffer themselves to be outdone by these racers or wrestlers? Can they use abstinence in diet, exert themselves in racing, expose their bodies to so much hardship in a combat, who have no more in view than the trifling huzzas of a giddy multitude, or a crown of leaves? And shall not Christians, who hope for the approbation of the sovereign Judge, and a crown of glory from his hands, stretch forward in the heavenly race, and exert themselves in beating down their fleshly inclinations, and the strong-holds of sin? 2. The racers in these games run at uncertainty. All run, but one receives the prize, <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.24">v. 24</reference>. Every racer, therefore, is at a great uncertainty whether he shall win it or no. But the Christian racer is at no such uncertainty. Every one may run here so as to obtain; but then he must run within the lines, he must keep to the path of duty prescribed, which, some think, is the meaning of <hi type="italic">running not as uncertainly,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.26">v. 26</reference>. He who keeps within the limits prescribed, and keeps on in his race, will never miss his crown, though others may get theirs before him. And would the Grecian racers keep within their bounds, and exert themselves to the very last, when one only could win, and all must be uncertain which that one would be? And shall not Christians be much more exact and vigorous when all are sure of a crown when they come to the end of their race? 3. He sets before himself and them the danger of yielding to fleshly inclinations, and pampering the body and its lusts and appetites: <hi type="italic">I keep my body under, lest that by any means, when I have preached to others, I myself should be a cast-away</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.9.27">v. 27</reference>), <hi type="italic">rejected, disapproved,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">adokimos,</hi></hi> one to whom the <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">brabeutes</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">the judge</hi> or <hi type="italic">umpire</hi> of the race, will not decree the crown. The allusion to the games runs through the whole sentence. Note, A preacher of salvation may yet miss it. He may show others the way to heaven, and never get thither himself. To prevent this, Paul took so much pains in subduing and keeping under bodily inclinations, lest by any means he himself, who had preached to others, should yet miss the crown, be disapproved and rejected by his sovereign Judge. A holy fear of himself was necessary to preserve the fidelity of an apostle; and how much more necessary is it to our preservation? Note, Holy fear of ourselves, and not presumptuous confidence, is the best security against apostasy from God, and final rejection by him.  <chapter eID="1Cor.9"/> <div eID="gen31196" type="x-p"/>

entries.1aa055eab92399a041204426782c55a06fc35fd8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16912"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 9</title> <div sID="gen33390" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.1-1Cor.9.27">1Co 9:1-27</reference>. He Confirms His Teaching as to Not Putting a Stumbling-block in a Brother's Way (<reference osisRef="1Cor.8.13">1Co 8:13</reference>) BY His Own Example in Not Using His Undoubted Rights as an Apostle, so as to Win Men to Christ.<div eID="gen33390" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33391" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16912"/><hi type="bold">1. Am I not an apostle? am I not free?--</hi>The oldest manuscripts read the order thus, "Am I not free? am I not an apostle?" He alludes to <reference osisRef="1Cor.8.9">1Co 8:9</reference>, "this liberty of yours": If you claim it, I appeal to yourselves as the witnesses, have not I also it? "Am I not free?" If you be so, much more I. For "am I not an apostle?" so that I can claim not only Christian, but also apostolic, liberty.<div eID="gen33391" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33392" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">have I not seen Jesus--</hi>corporeally, not in a mere vision: compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.8">1Co 15:8</reference>, where the fact of the resurrection, which he wishes to prove, could only be established by an actual bodily appearance, such as was vouchsafed to Peter and the other apostles. In <reference osisRef="Acts.9.7">Ac 9:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.9.17">17</reference> the contrast between "the men with him seeing no man," and "Jesus that appeared unto thee in the way," shows that Jesus actually appeared to him in going to Damascus. His vision of Christ in the temple (<reference osisRef="Acts.22.17">Ac 22:17</reference>) was "in a trance." To be a witness of Christ's resurrection was a leading function of an apostle (<reference osisRef="Acts.1.22">Ac 1:22</reference>). The best manuscripts omit "Christ."<div eID="gen33392" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33393" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ye my work in the Lord--</hi>Your conversion is His workmanship (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.10">Ep 2:10</reference>) through my instrumentality: the "seal of mine apostleship" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.9.2">1Co 9:2</reference>). <div eID="gen33393" type="x-p"/>
entries.5ffac0bde9a16358766d5c74f254377e01d9f5b8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16913"/><div sID="gen33394" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16913"/><hi type="bold">2. yet doubtless--</hi>yet at least I am such to you.<div eID="gen33394" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33395" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">seal of mine apostleship--</hi>Your conversion by my preaching, accompanied with miracles ("the signs of an apostle," <reference osisRef="Rom.15.18">Ro 15:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.15.19">19</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.12">2Co 12:12</reference>), and your gifts conferred by me (<reference osisRef="1Cor.1.7">1Co 1:7</reference>), vouch for the reality of my apostleship, just as a seal set to a document attests its genuineness (<reference osisRef="John.3.33">Joh 3:33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.4.11">Ro 4:11</reference>). <div eID="gen33395" type="x-p"/>
entries.9b7d22a7c351668548452096b70aa121b90c8af3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16914"/><div sID="gen33396" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16914"/><hi type="bold">3. to them that ... examine me--</hi>that is, who call in question mine apostleship.<div eID="gen33396" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33397" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">is this--</hi>namely, that you are the seal of mine apostleship. <div eID="gen33397" type="x-p"/>
entries.c0658b8ee2ea62a9f701519fc11b0bc7a30ba0cd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16915"/><div sID="gen33398" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16915"/><hi type="bold">4. Have we not power--</hi>Greek, "right," or lawful power, equivalent to "liberty" claimed by the Corinthians (<reference osisRef="1Cor.8.9">1Co 8:9</reference>). The "we" includes with himself his colleagues in the apostleship. The Greek interrogative expresses, "You surely won't say (will you?) that we have not the power or right," &c.<div eID="gen33398" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33399" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">eat and drink--</hi>without laboring with our hands (<reference osisRef="1Cor.9.11">1Co 9:11</reference>, 13, 14). Paul's not exercising this right was made a plea by his opponents for insinuating that he was himself conscious he was no true apostle (<reference osisRef="2Cor.12.13-2Cor.12.16">2Co 12:13-16</reference>). <div eID="gen33399" type="x-p"/>
entries.51d3676ce1d984bb124d133d6155bfd461608d0f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16916"/><div sID="gen33400" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16916"/><hi type="bold">5. lead about a sister, a wife--</hi>that is, "a sister as a wife"; "a sister" by faith, which makes all believers brethren and sisters in the one family of God: "a wife" by marriage covenant. Paul implies he did not exercise his undoubted right to marry and "lead about" a believer, for the sake of Christian expediency, as well to save the Church the expense of maintaining her in his wide circuits, as also that he might give himself more undistractedly to building up the Church of Christ (<reference osisRef="1Cor.7.26">1Co 7:26</reference>, 32, 35). Contrast the Corinthians' want of self-sacrifice in the exercise of their "liberty" at the cost of destroying, instead of edifying, the Church (<reference osisRef="1Cor.8.9">1Co 8:9</reference>, Margin; <reference osisRef="1Cor.8.10-1Cor.8.13">1Co 8:10-13</reference>).<div eID="gen33400" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33401" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as other apostles--</hi>implying that some of them had availed themselves of the power which they all had, of marrying. We know from <reference osisRef="Matt.8.14">Mt 8:14</reference>, that Cephas (Peter) was a married man. A confutation of Peter's self-styled followers, the Romanists, who exclude the clergy from marriage. Clement of Alexandria [Miscellanies, 7.63] records a tradition that he encouraged his wife when being led to death by saying, "Remember, my dear one, the Lord." Compare Eusebius [Eccleiastical History, 3.30].<div eID="gen33401" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33402" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">brethren of the Lord--</hi>held in especial esteem on account of their relationship to Jesus (<reference osisRef="Acts.1.14">Ac 1:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.1.9">Ga 1:9</reference>). James, Joses, Simon, and Judas. Probably cousins of Jesus: as cousins were termed by the Jews "brethren." Alford makes them literally brothers of Jesus by Joseph and Mary.<div eID="gen33402" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33403" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Cephas--</hi>probably singled out as being a name carrying weight with one partisan section at Corinth. "If your favorite leader does so, surely so may I" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.1.12">1Co 1:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.22">3:22</reference>). <div eID="gen33403" type="x-p"/>
entries.4731792277aeac0665eb17ef3d8cef00241623ad: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16917"/><div sID="gen33404" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16917"/><hi type="bold">6. Barnabas--</hi>long the associate of Paul, and, like him, in the habit of self-denyingly forbearing to claim the maintenance which is a minister's right. So Paul supported himself by tent-making (<reference osisRef="Acts.18.3">Ac 18:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.20.34">20:34</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.9">1Th 2:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Thess.3.8">2Th 3:8</reference>). <div eID="gen33404" type="x-p"/>
entries.0556e7a96db7e09f2daa76d85d14a74217903ed3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16918"/><div sID="gen33405" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16918"/>7. The minister is spiritually a soldier (<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.3">2Ti 2:3</reference>), a vine-dresser (<reference osisRef="1Cor.3.6-1Cor.3.8">1Co 3:6-8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Song.1.6">So 1:6</reference>), and a shepherd (<reference osisRef="1Pet.5.2">1Pe 5:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Pet.5.4">4</reference>).<div eID="gen33405" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33406" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of the fruit--</hi>The oldest manuscripts omit "of." <div eID="gen33406" type="x-p"/>
entries.d5a2a25bd26b96845974e58c5f5c6e67e4c560e5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16919"/><div sID="gen33407" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16919"/><hi type="bold">8. as a man--</hi>I speak thus not merely according to human judgment, but with the sanction of the divine law also. <div eID="gen33407" type="x-p"/>
entries.863ae0343aef800a00516f1cc1cdda7a11a7b5c0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16920"/><div sID="gen33408" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16920"/><hi type="bold">9. ox ... treadeth ... corn--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Deut.25.4">De 25:4</reference>). In the East to the present day they do not after reaping carry the sheaves home to barns as we do, but take them to an area under the open air to be threshed by the oxen treading them with their feet, or else drawing a threshing instrument over them (compare <reference osisRef="Mic.4.13">Mi 4:13</reference>).<div eID="gen33408" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33409" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Doth God ... care for oxen?--</hi>rather, "Is it for the oxen that God careth?" Is the animal the ultimate object for whose sake this law was given? No. God does care for the lower animal (<reference osisRef="Ps.36.6">Psa 36:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.10.29">Mt 10:29</reference>), but it is with the ultimate aim of the welfare of man, the head of animal creation. In the humane consideration shown for the lower animal, we are to learn that still more ought it to be exercised in the case of man, the ultimate object of the law; and that the human (spiritual as well as temporal) laborer is worthy of his hire. <div eID="gen33409" type="x-p"/>
entries.c47c6207cab0328cd7cb62fdf43948fe7cbccf44: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16921"/><div sID="gen33410" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16921"/><hi type="bold">10. altogether--</hi>Join this with "saith." "Does he (the divine lawgiver) by all means say it for our sakes?" It would be untrue, that God saith it altogether (in the sense of solely) for our sakes. But it is true, that He by all means saith it for our sakes as the ultimate object in the lower world. Grotius, however, translates, "mainly" or "especially," instead of altogether.<div eID="gen33410" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33411" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that--</hi>"meaning that" [Alford]; literally, "because."<div eID="gen33411" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33412" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">should plough--</hi>ought to plough in hope. The obligation rests with the people not to let their minister labor without remuneration.<div eID="gen33412" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33413" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he that thresheth in hope should be partaker of his hope--</hi>The oldest manuscript versions and Fathers read, "He that thresheth (should or ought to thresh) in the hope of partaking" (namely, of the fruit of his threshing). "He that plougheth," spiritually, is the first planter of a church in a place (compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.6">1Co 3:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.9">9</reference>); "he that thresheth," the minister who tends a church already planted. <div eID="gen33413" type="x-p"/>
entries.a475141704e999b32d1de620a92b13fbed161fb7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16922"/><div sID="gen33414" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16922"/><hi type="bold">11. we ... we--</hi>emphatical in the Greek. We, the same persons who have sown to you the infinitely more precious treasures of the Spirit, may at least claim in return what is the only thing you have to give, namely, the goods that nourish the flesh ("your carnal things"). <div eID="gen33414" type="x-p"/>
entries.30e8da02acd1b8ef8970cb6d95db228e5d6efc76: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16923"/><div sID="gen33415" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16923"/><hi type="bold">12. others--</hi>whether true apostles (<reference osisRef="1Cor.9.5">1Co 9:5</reference>) or false ones (<reference osisRef="2Cor.11.20">2Co 11:20</reference>).<div eID="gen33415" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33416" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">we rather--</hi>considering our greater labors for you (<reference osisRef="2Cor.11.23">2Co 11:23</reference>).<div eID="gen33416" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33417" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">suffer all things--</hi>without complaining of it. We desire to conceal (literally, "hold as a water-tight vessel") any distress we suffer from straitened circumstances. The same Greek is in <reference osisRef="1Cor.13.7">1Co 13:7</reference>.<div eID="gen33417" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33418" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lest we ... hinder ... gospel--</hi>not to cause a hindrance to its progress by giving a handle for the imputation of self-seeking, if we received support from our flock. The less of incumbrance and expense caused to the Church, and the more of work done, the better for the cause of the Gospel (<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.4">2Ti 2:4</reference>). <div eID="gen33418" type="x-p"/>
entries.47fbf3afbd27aa0366d8f3473dab75d1d2482b9e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16924"/><div sID="gen33419" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16924"/><hi type="bold">13. minister about holy things--</hi>the Jewish priests and Levites. The Greek especially applies to the former, the priests offering sacrifices.<div eID="gen33419" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33420" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">partakers with the altar--</hi>a part of the victims going to the service of the altar, and the rest being shared by the priests (<reference osisRef="Lev.7.6">Le 7:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.18.6">Nu 18:6</reference>, &c.; <reference osisRef="Deut.18.1">De 18:1</reference>, &c.). <div eID="gen33420" type="x-p"/>
entries.156e08bcd2031f5112f2d6f40b00559b07f47a0b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16925"/><div sID="gen33421" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16925"/><hi type="bold">14. Even so--</hi>The only inference to be drawn from this passage is, not that the Christian ministry is of a sacrificial character as the Jewish priesthood, but simply, that as the latter was supported by the contributions of the people, so should the former. The stipends of the clergy were at first from voluntary offerings at the Lord's Supper. At the love-feast preceding it every believer, according to his ability, offered a gift; and when the expense of the table had been defrayed, the bishop laid aside a portion for himself, the presbyters, and deacons; and with the rest relieved widows, orphans, confessors, and the poor generally [Tertullian, Apology, 39]. The stipend was in proportion to the dignity and merits of the several bishops, presbyters, and deacons [Cyprian, c. 4, ep. 6].<div eID="gen33421" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33422" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">preach ... gospel--</hi>plainly marked as the duty of the Christian minister, in contrast to the ministering about sacrifices (Greek) and waiting at the altar of the Jewish priesthood and Levites (<reference osisRef="1Cor.9.13">1Co 9:13</reference>). If the Lord's Supper were a sacrifice (as the Mass is supposed to be), this fourteenth verse would certainly have been worded so, to answer to <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.13">1Co 9:13</reference>. Note the same Lord Christ "ordains" the ordinances in the Old and in the New Testaments (<reference osisRef="Matt.10.10">Mt 10:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.10.7">Lu 10:7</reference>). <div eID="gen33422" type="x-p"/>
entries.98acbc526113693d9dddb3c3af48ca4591f1c853: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16926"/><div sID="gen33423" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16926"/>15. Paul's special gift of continency, which enabled him to abstain from marriage, and his ability to maintain himself without interrupting seriously his ministry, made that expedient to him which is ordinarily inexpedient; namely, that the ministry should not be supported by the people. What to him was a duty, would be the opposite to one, for instance, to whom God had committed a family, without other means of support.<div eID="gen33423" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33424" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I have used none of these things--</hi>none of these "powers" or rights which I might have used (<reference osisRef="1Cor.9.4-1Cor.6.12">1Co 9:4-6, 12</reference>).<div eID="gen33424" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33425" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">neither--</hi>rather, "Yet I have not written."<div eID="gen33425" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33426" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">so done unto me--</hi>literally, "in my case": as is done in the case of a soldier, a planter, a shepherd, a ploughman, and a sacrificing priest (<reference osisRef="1Cor.9.7">1Co 9:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.13">10, 13</reference>).<div eID="gen33426" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33427" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">make my glorying void--</hi>deprive me of my privilege of preaching the Gospel without remuneration (<reference osisRef="2Cor.11.7-2Cor.11.10">2Co 11:7-10</reference>). Rather than hinder the progress of the Gospel by giving any pretext for a charge of interested motives (<reference osisRef="2Cor.12.17">2Co 12:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.18">18</reference>), Paul would "die" of hunger. Compare Abraham's similar disinterestedness (<reference osisRef="Gen.14.22">Ge 14:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.14.23">23</reference>). <div eID="gen33427" type="x-p"/>
entries.d9d25662c539c019d21d90349317bdbd17735e74: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16927"/><div sID="gen33428" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16927"/><hi type="bold">16. though I preach ... I have nothing to glory of--</hi>that is, If I preach the Gospel, and do so not gratuitously, I have no matter for "glorying." For the "necessity" that is laid on me to preach (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.20.9">Jr 20:9</reference>, and the case of Jonah) does away with ground for "glorying." The sole ground for the latter that I have, is my preaching without charge (<reference osisRef="1Cor.9.18">1Co 9:18</reference>): since there is no necessity laid on me as to the latter, it is my voluntary act for the Gospel's sake. <div eID="gen33428" type="x-p"/>
entries.22e8ffe0b050b238fd25c3c2405da5e0cfec48c7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16928"/><div sID="gen33429" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16928"/>17. Translate, "If I be doing this (that is, preaching) of my own accord (which I am not, for the 'necessity' is laid on me which binds a servant to obey his master), I have a reward; but if (as is the case) involuntarily (<reference osisRef="Acts.9.15">Ac 9:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.22.15">22:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.26.16">26:16</reference>); not of my own natural will, but by the constraining grace of God; (<reference osisRef="Rom.9.16">Ro 9:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.13-1Tim.1.16">1Ti 1:13-16</reference>), I have had a dispensation (of the Gospel) entrusted to me" (and so can claim no "reward," seeing that I only "have done that which was my duty to do," <reference osisRef="Luke.17.10">Lu 17:10</reference>, but incur the "woe," <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.16">1Co 9:16</reference>, if I fail in it). <div eID="gen33429" type="x-p"/>
entries.205d8f52091ef7f6251a95ee414c72df19631161: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16929"/><div sID="gen33430" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16929"/><hi type="bold">18. What is my reward?--</hi>The answer is in <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.19">1Co 9:19</reference>; namely, that by making the Gospel without charge, where I might have rightfully claimed maintenance, I might "win the more."<div eID="gen33430" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33431" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of Christ--</hi>The oldest manuscripts and versions omit these words.<div eID="gen33431" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33432" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">abuse--</hi>rather "that I use not to the full my power." This is his matter for "glorying"; the "reward" ultimately aimed at is the gaining of the more (<reference osisRef="1Cor.9.19">1Co 9:19</reference>). The former, as involving the latter, is verbally made the answer to the question, "What is my reward?" But really the "reward" is that which is the ultimate aim of his preaching without charge, namely, that he may gain the more; it was for this end, not to have matter of glorying, that he did so. <div eID="gen33432" type="x-p"/>
entries.8371351f68c3796077ff79c205dd1a152fd8ac9e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16930"/><div sID="gen33433" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16930"/><hi type="bold">19. free from all men--</hi>that is, from the power of all men.<div eID="gen33433" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33434" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">gain the more--</hi>that is, as many of them ("all men") as possible. "Gain" is an appropriate expression in relation to a "reward" (<reference osisRef="1Thess.2.19">1Th 2:19</reference>, 20); he therefore repeats it frequently (<reference osisRef="1Cor.9.20-1Cor.9.22">1Co 9:20-22</reference>). <div eID="gen33434" type="x-p"/>
entries.0b07b3d49a2af1ff2449989c5bbb422c02357a20: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16931"/><div sID="gen33435" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16931"/><hi type="bold">20. I became as a Jew--</hi>in things not defined by the law, but by Jewish usage. Not Judaizing in essentials, but in matters where there was no compromise of principle (compare <reference osisRef="Acts.16.3">Ac 16:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.21.20-Acts.21.26">21:20-26</reference>); an undesigned coincidence between the history and the Epistle, and so a sure proof of genuineness.<div eID="gen33435" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33436" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to them that are under the law, as under the law--</hi>in things defined by the law; such as ceremonies not then repugnant to Christianity. Perhaps the reason for distinguishing this class from the former is that Paul himself belonged nationally to "the Jews," but did not in creed belong to the class of "them that are under the law." This view is confirmed by the reading inserted here by the oldest manuscripts, versions, and Fathers, "not being (that is, parenthetically, 'not that I am') myself under the law." <div eID="gen33436" type="x-p"/>
entries.58cf77d86460b7f23bd3e388b65e986222e925bb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16932"/><div sID="gen33437" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16932"/><hi type="bold">21. To them ... without law--</hi>that is, without revealed law: the heathen (compare <reference osisRef="Rom.2.12">Ro 2:12</reference> with <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.15">1Co 9:15</reference>).<div eID="gen33437" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33438" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as without law--</hi>not urging on them the ceremonies and "works of the law," but "the hearing of faith" (<reference osisRef="Gal.3.2">Ga 3:2</reference>). Also discoursing in their own manner, as at Athens, with arguments from their own poets (<reference osisRef="Acts.17.28">Ac 17:28</reference>).<div eID="gen33438" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33439" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">being not without law to God--</hi>"While thus conforming to others in matters indifferent, taking care not to be without law in relation to God, but responsible to law (literally, "IN LAW") in relation to Christ." This is the Christian's true position in relation to the world, to himself, and to God. Everything develops itself according to its proper law. So the Christian, though no longer subject to the literal law as constraining him from without, is subject to an inward principle or law, the spirit of faith in Christ acting from within as the germ of a new life. He does not in the Greek (as in English Version) say "under the law (as he does in <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.20">1Co 9:20</reference>) to Christ"; but uses the milder term, "in ... law," responsible to law. Christ was responsible to the law for us, so that we are no longer responsible to it (<reference osisRef="Gal.3.13">Ga 3:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gal.3.24">24</reference>), but to Him, as the members to the Head (<reference osisRef="1Cor.7.22">1Co 7:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.8.1-Rom.8.4">Ro 8:1-4</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.16">1Pe 2:16</reference>). Christians serve Christ in newness of spirit, no longer in oldness of the letter (that is, the old external law as such), <reference osisRef="Rom.7.4-Rom.7.6">Ro 7:4-6</reference>. To Christ, as man's Head, the Father has properly delegated His authority (<reference osisRef="John.5.22">Joh 5:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.5.27">27</reference>); whence here he substitutes "Christ" for "God" in the second clause, "not without law to God, but under the law to Christ." The law of Christ is the law of love (<reference osisRef="Gal.6.2">Ga 6:2</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Gal.5.13">Ga 5:13</reference>). <div eID="gen33439" type="x-p"/>
entries.67e09f48461bd54001eed2bc636a0582fdefceac: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16933"/><div sID="gen33440" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16933"/><hi type="bold">22. gain the weak--</hi>that is, establish, instead of being a stumbling-block to inexperienced Christians (<reference osisRef="1Cor.8.7">1Co 8:7</reference>) <reference osisRef="Rom.14.1">Ro 14:1</reference>, "Weak in the faith." Alford thinks the "weak" are not Christians at all, for these have been already "won"; but those outside the Church, who are yet "without strength" to believe (<reference osisRef="Rom.5.6">Ro 5:6</reference>). But when "weak" Christians are by the condescending love of stronger brethren kept from falling from faith, they are well said to be "gained" or won.<div eID="gen33440" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33441" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by all means ... some--</hi>The gain of even "some" is worth the expenditure of "all means." He conformed himself to the feelings of each in the several classes, that out of them all he might gain some. <div eID="gen33441" type="x-p"/>
entries.b09a4c28ca5ca168847bd3d98c350031f26dd711: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16934"/><div sID="gen33442" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16934"/><hi type="bold">23. partaker thereof--</hi>Greek, "fellow partaker": of the Gospel blessings promised at Christ's coming: "with" (not as English Version, "you": but) them, namely, with those thus "gained" by me to the Gospel. <div eID="gen33442" type="x-p"/>
entries.a97b667d2d9ac1849f983514571813235c05e65d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16935"/><div sID="gen33443" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16935"/><hi type="bold">24. Know ye not--</hi>The Isthmian games, in which the foot race was a leading one, were of course well known, and a subject of patriotic pride to the Corinthians, who lived in the immediate neighborhood. These periodical games were to the Greeks rather a passion than a mere amusement: hence their suitableness as an image of Christian earnestness.<div eID="gen33443" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33444" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in a race--</hi>Greek, "in a race course."<div eID="gen33444" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33445" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all ... one--</hi>Although we knew that one alone could be saved, still it Would be well worth our while to run [Bengel]. Even in the Christian race not "all" who enter on the race win (<reference osisRef="1Cor.10.1-1Cor.10.5">1Co 10:1-5</reference>).<div eID="gen33445" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33446" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">So run, that ye may obtain--</hi>said parenthetically. These are the words in which the instructors of the young in the exercise schools (gymnasia) and the spectators on the race course exhorted their pupils to stimulate them to put forth all exertions. The gymnasium was a prominent feature in every Greek city. Every candidate had to take an oath that he had been ten months in training, and that he would violate none of the regulations (<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.5">2Ti 2:5</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.7">1Ti 4:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.8">8</reference>). He lived on a strict self-denying diet, refraining from wine and pleasant foods, and enduring cold and heat and most laborious discipline. The "prize" awarded by the judge or umpire was a chaplet of green leaves; at the Isthmus, those of the indigenous pine, for which parsley leaves were temporarily substituted (<reference osisRef="1Cor.9.25">1Co 9:25</reference>). The Greek for "obtain" is fully obtain. It is in vain to begin, unless we persevere to the end (<reference osisRef="Matt.10.22">Mt 10:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.24.13">24:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.2.10">Re 2:10</reference>). The "so" expresses, Run with such perseverance in the heavenly course, as "all" the runners exhibit in the earthly "race" just spoken of: to the end that ye may attain the prize. <div eID="gen33446" type="x-p"/>
entries.7d60f5902622866d7a86cee893982d531776b435: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16936"/><div sID="gen33447" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16936"/><hi type="bold">25. striveth--</hi>in wrestling: a still more severe contest than the foot race.<div eID="gen33447" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33448" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">is temperate--</hi>So Paul exercised self-denial, abstaining from claiming sustenance for the sake of the "reward," namely, to "gain the more" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.9.18">1Co 9:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.19">19</reference>).<div eID="gen33448" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33449" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">corruptible--</hi>soon withering, as being only of fir leaves taken from the fir groves which surrounded the Isthmian race course or stadium.<div eID="gen33449" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33450" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">incorruptible--</hi>(<reference osisRef="1Pet.1.4">1Pe 1:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.5.4">5:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.2.10">Re 2:10</reference>). "Crown" here is not that of a king (which is expressed by a different Greek word, namely, "diadem"), but a wreath or garland. <div eID="gen33450" type="x-p"/>
entries.35b58f37487559c974f80e30b3e72f07663c2a22: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16937"/><div sID="gen33451" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16937"/><hi type="bold">26. I--</hi>Paul returns to his main subject, his own self-denial, and his motive in it.<div eID="gen33451" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33452" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">run, not as uncertainly--</hi>not as a runner uncertain of the goal. Ye Corinthians gain no end in your entering idol temples or eating idol meats. But I, for my part, in all my acts, whether in my becoming "all things to all men," or in receiving no sustenance from my converts, have a definite end in view, namely, to "gain the more." I know what 1 aim at, and how to aim at it. He who runs with a clear aim, looks straightforward to the goal, makes it his sole aim, casts away every encumbrance (<reference osisRef="Heb.12.1">He 12:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.2">2</reference>), is indifferent to what the by-standers say, and sometimes even a fall only serves to rouse him the more [Bengel].<div eID="gen33452" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33453" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not as one that beateth the air--</hi>instead of beating the adversary. Alluding to the sciamachia or sparring in the school in sham-fight (compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.9">1Co 14:9</reference>), wherein they struck out into the air as if at an imaginary adversary. The real adversary is Satan acting on us through the flesh. <div eID="gen33453" type="x-p"/>
entries.a5e062ce8cb12b3365ebcdc22a38efcc80bd0178: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16938"/><div sID="gen33454" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16938"/><hi type="bold">27. keep under--</hi>literally, "bruise the face under the eyes," so as to render it black and blue; so, to chastise in the most sensitive part. Compare "mortify the deeds of the body," <reference osisRef="Rom.8.13">Ro 8:13</reference>; also <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.11">1Pe 2:11</reference>. It is not ascetic fasts or macerations of the body which are here recommended, but the keeping under of our natural self-seeking, so as, like Paul, to lay ourselves out entirely for the great work.<div eID="gen33454" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33455" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">my body--</hi>the old man and the remainders of lust in my flesh. "My body," so far as by the flesh it opposes the spirit [Estius] (<reference osisRef="Gal.5.17">Ga 5:17</reference>). Men may be severe to their bodies and yet indulge their lust. Ascetic "neglect of the body" may be all the while a more subtile "satisfying of the flesh" (<reference osisRef="Col.2.23">Col 2:23</reference>). Unless the soul keep the body under, the body will get above the soul. The body may be made a good servant, but is a bad master.<div eID="gen33455" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33456" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bring it into subjection--</hi>or bondage, as a slave or servant led away captive; so the Greek.<div eID="gen33456" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33457" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">preached--</hi>literally, "heralded." He keeps up the image from the races. The heralds summoned the candidates for the foot race into the race course [Plato, Laws, 8.833], and placed the crowns on the brows of the conquerors, announcing their names [Bengel]. They probably proclaimed also the laws of the combat; answering to the preaching of the apostles [Alford]. The The Christian herald is also a combatant, in which respect he is distinguished from the herald at the games.<div eID="gen33457" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33458" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a castaway--</hi>failing shamefully of the prize myself, after I have called others to the contest. Rejected by God, the Judge of the Christian race, notwithstanding my having, by my preaching, led others to be accepted. Compare the equivalent term, "reprobate," <reference osisRef="Jer.6.30">Jr 6:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.13.6">2Co 13:6</reference>. Paul implies, if such earnest, self-denying watchfulness over himself be needed still, with all his labors for others, to make his own calling sure, much more is the same needed by the Corinthians, instead of their going, as they do, to the extreme limit of Christian liberty. <chapter eID="1Cor.9"/>

entries.9fadbe3c8c54f7759b1b03b3770de240e7af3d42: <div eID="gen47748" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen47749" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen47750" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen47750" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen47749" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen47751" type="x-p"/> St. Paul vindicates his apostleship, and shows that he has equal rights and privileges with Peter and the brethren of our Lord; and that he is not bound, while doing the work of an apostle, to labor with his hands for his own support, <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.1-1Cor.9.6">1Cor 9:1-6</reference>. He who labors should live by the fruit of his own industry, <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.7">1Cor 9:7</reference>. For the law will not allow even the ox to be muzzled which treads out the corn, <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.8-1Cor.9.10">1Cor 9:8-10</reference>. Those who minister in spiritual things have a right to a secular support for their work, <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.11-1Cor.9.14">1Cor 9:11-14</reference>. He shows the disinterested manner in which he has preached the Gospel, <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.15-1Cor.9.18">1Cor 9:15-18</reference>. Now he accommodated himself to the prejudices of men, in order to bring about their salvation, <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.19-1Cor.9.23">1Cor 9:19-23</reference>. The way to heaven compared to a race, <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.24">1Cor 9:24</reference>. The qualifications of those who may expect success in the games celebrated at Corinth, and what that success implies, <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.25">1Cor 9:25</reference>. The apostle applies these things spiritually to himself; and states the necessity of keeping his body in subjection, lest, after having proclaimed salvation to others, he should become a castaway, <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.26">1Cor 9:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.27">1Cor 9:27</reference>. <div eID="gen47751" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47752" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen47752" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47753" type="x-p"/> Am I not an apostle? - It is sufficiently evident that there were persons at Corinth who questioned the apostleship of St. Paul; and he was obliged to walk very circumspectly that they might not find any occasion against him. It appears also that he had given them all his apostolical labors gratis; and even this, which was the highest proof of his disinterested benevolence, was produced by his opposers as an argument against him. "Prophets, and all divinely commissioned men, have a right to their secular support; you take nothing: - is not this from a conviction that you have no apostolical right?" On this point the apostle immediately enters on his own defense. <div eID="gen47753" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47754" type="x-p"/> Am I not an apostle? Am I not free? - These questions are all designed as assertions of the affirmative: I am an apostle; and I am free - possessed of all the rights and privileges of an apostle. <div eID="gen47754" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47755" type="x-p"/> Have I not seen Jesus Christ - From whom in his personal appearance to me, I have received my apostolic commission. This was judged essentially necessary to constitute an apostle. See <reference osisRef="Act.22.14">Act 22:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Act.22.15">Act 22:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Act.26.16">Act 26:16</reference>. <div eID="gen47755" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47756" type="x-p"/> Are not ye my work - Your conversion from heathenism is the proof that I have preached with the Divine unction and authority. <div eID="gen47756" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47757" type="x-p"/> Several good MSS. and versions transpose the two first questions in this verse, thus: Am I not free? am I not an apostle? But I cannot see that either perspicuity or sense gains any thing by this arrangement. On the contrary, it appears to me that his being an apostle gave him the freedom or rights to which he refers, and therefore the common arrangement I judge to be the best.
entries.a38f88845ca8afd1d8e8e3d886c2bcfdd761a5a3: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen47757" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47758" type="x-p"/> If I be not an apostle unto others - If there be other Churches which have been founded by other apostles; yet it is not so with you. <div eID="gen47758" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47759" type="x-p"/> The seal of mine apostleship are ye - Your conversion to Christianity is God's seal to my apostleship. Had not God sent me, I could not have profited your souls. <div eID="gen47759" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47760" type="x-p"/> The σφραγις or seal, was a figure cut in a stone, and that set in a ring, by which letters of credence and authority were stamped. The ancients, particularly the Greeks, excelled in this kind of engraving. The cabinets of the curious give ample proof of this; and the moderns contend in vain to rival the perfection of those ancient masters. <div eID="gen47760" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47761" type="x-p"/> In the Lord - The apostle shows that it was by the grace and influence of God alone that he was an apostle, and that they were converted to Christianity.
entries.f884077356de729ea96ee09c55cbc028d3a54ac0: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen47761" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47762" type="x-p"/> Mine answer to them - Ἡ εμη απολογια τοις εμε ανακρινουσιν· This is my defense against those who examine me. The words are forensic; and the apostle considers himself as brought before a legal tribunal, and questioned so as to be obliged to answer as upon oath. His defense therefore was this, that they were converted to God by his means. This verse belongs to the two preceding verses.
entries.e9253e160bdb85b0f85f3716af1af59d34275198: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen47762" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47763" type="x-p"/> Have we not power to eat and to drink? - Have we not authority, or right, εξουσιαν, to expect sustenance, while we are labouring for your salvation? Meat and drink, the necessaries, not the superfluities, of life, were what those primitive messengers of Christ required; it was just that they who labored in the Gospel should live by the Gospel; they did not wish to make a fortune, or accumulate wealth; a living was all they desired. It was probably in reference to the same moderate and reasonable desire that the provision made for the clergy in this country was called a living; and their work for which they got this living was called the cure of souls.
