<ns0:div xmlns:ns0="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="9" type="chapter">
               <ns0:head>CHAP. IX.</ns0:head>
               <ns0:p n="1">1 AM I not an Apostle? <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Some that are puffed up or <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>educed, will, it may be, de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ny that I am an <ns0:hi>Apostle,</ns0:hi> a Preacher of the Gospel of the greatest eminency, immediately sent out by Christ to preach his Gospel, but will any of you deny it?</ns0:note>, am I not free? <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Have not I the same liberty that any of you have in things wherein the Law of God hath no more determined me than you? What Charter of liberty hath God given to any of you more than he hath to me?</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 15.8.</ns0:note> have not I seen Jesus Christ our Lord? <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Have I not seen Jesus Christ? <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 10.41. Did not I see Christ in my going to <ns0:hi>Damascus? Acts</ns0:hi> 9.5. And when I was in my ecstasie? <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 22.13, 14. When I was rapt into the third Heavens? 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 12.1, 2. In prison? <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 23.11. He was the only Apostle we read of, who saw Christ after his Ascen<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sion.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 4.15.</ns0:note> are not you my work in the Lord? <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">If others will not look upon me as an Apostle, God having wrought nothing upon their Souls by my Ministry, yet you whose Faith is my work, though in the Lord, as the prin<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cipal efficient Cause, yet by me as Gods instrument, cannot deny me to be so, if my having seen Jesus Christ, and being immediately sent out by him, be not enough to prove me so to you, yet the effects of my Ministry upon you puts it past your denial.</ns0:note>.<ns0:note place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>In the greater part of this Chapter, the Apostle proceedeth in his former discourse, not speaking particularly to the case of eating meat offered to Idols, but to the general point,</ns0:hi> viz. <ns0:hi>That it is our duty to abate of our liberty, when we see we cannot use it without harm to other Christians. And here he proposeth to them his own example, who had restrained himself in three things, to two of which he had a liberty, and yet avoided it, and that not to prevent their sinning, but only their suffering, and that too only by being by him over-burthened</ns0:hi>; 1. <ns0:hi>As to eating and drinking.</ns0:hi> 2. <ns0:hi>Abstaining from marriage, by which he might have been more chargeable to them.</ns0:hi> 3. <ns0:hi>Requiring maintenance of them for his labour amongst them. As to both which he de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />clares he had from Gods Law a liberty, but had forborn to use that part from which the Church in that state might be prejudiced.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="2">2 If I be not an apostle unto others, yet doubt<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />less I am to you <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">He had, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 1. told them they were his <ns0:hi>work in th<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> Lord;</ns0:hi> from whence he concludes here, That he was an <ns0:hi>Apostle,</ns0:hi> that is, one sent of Christ to them for the good of their Souls, whatever he was to others.</ns0:note>: for the <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">2 Cor. 12.1<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>
                  </ns0:note> seal of my apostleship are ye in the Lord <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">You, saith he, as to your selves at least are the <ns0:hi>Seal</ns0:hi> of my Apostolical Office, it hath a confirmation in you by the effect, as the writing is confirmed by the seal. For how can you think, that the blessing of the Lord should go a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />long with my preaching, to turn you from Pagan Idolatry, and your lewd courses of life to the true Christian Religion, and to an holy life and conversation, if God had not sent me. There is no such Argument to prove a Minister sent of Christ, as the success of his Ministry in the conversion of Souls unto God. It is true, we cannot conclude, That a Minister is no true Mini<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ster, if he be able to produce no such seals of his calling. For the spiritual seed may for a time lie under the clods, and changes may be wrought in hearts, which are not published to the world: and even <ns0:hi>Isaiah</ns0:hi> may be sent to make the <ns0:hi>hearts of people fat.</ns0:hi> But where those seals can be produced, it is a most certain sign, that the Minister is a true Minister, that is, one sent of God; for he could be no instrument to do such works, if God were not with him: and if God had not sent him, he would not be with him so blessing his Ministry; yet it is possible the man may have his personal errours: For though some men doubt, whether an instance can be given of one openly and scandalously wicked, whom God ever honoured to be his instrument to convert Souls, yet it would be rashly affir<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />med by any to say, That <ns0:hi>Iudas</ns0:hi> (though a son of perdition, but not scandalous till the last) was an instrument to convert none.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="3">3 Mine answer to them that do examine me is this <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">These words may be understood in a double reference: either to what went before, then the sense is this: To those that examine me about my Apostleship, this is <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> answer; <ns0:hi>That I have seen the Lord, That you are my work in the Lord,</ns0:hi> and the <ns0:hi>Seal of my Ministry.</ns0:hi> Or with reference to the words that follow, then the sense is this: If any man examine me, how I my self practise the Doctrine which I preach to others, and de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />termine my self as to my liberty for the good and profit of o<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thers? I give them the following answer.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="4">4 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Vers. 14. 1 Thess. 2.6. 2 Thess. 3.9.</ns0:note> Have we not power to eat and to drink? <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Could I not eat and drink of such things offered to Idols as well as you? Have not I as great a knowledge, and as much liberty? Yet you see I forbear. But the generality of Inter<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />preters rather incline to interpret it by what followeth: Then, though it be here shortly expressed, and more fully opened af<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />terward, yet the sense is: Have not I power to ask a mainte<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nance of you, by which I should be inabled to eat and drink.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="5">5 Have we not power to lead about a sister, a <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 span">
                        <ns0:desc>〈…〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> wife <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Those that by those terms, <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, understand, not (as we translate it) a sister, a wife, but a <ns0:hi>woman,</ns0:hi> that should out of her estate have contributed to the Apostles main<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tenance (as <ns0:hi>Ioanna the wife of Chuza, Herods Steward,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Su<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sanna,</ns0:hi> and many others followed <ns0:hi>Christ, ministring to him of their substance,</ns0:hi> Luke 8.3.) seem not to consider: 1. That such women would have been no burden, but an help to the Church (which is quite contrary to the Apostles sense.) 2. That the term <ns0:hi>leading about,</ns0:hi> imports a conjugal relation to the woman. 3. That if this had been the sense, it had been enough to have said, to <ns0:hi>lead about a woman,</ns0:hi> he should not need have said, a <ns0:hi>sister,</ns0:hi> a <ns0:hi>woman.</ns0:hi> 4. That such leading about a woman, not their wife, had been scandalous. 5. That the very phrase, a <ns0:hi>sister,</ns0:hi> a <ns0:hi>wife,</ns0:hi> answers the phrase, <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 23.1. <ns0:hi>Men, brethren,</ns0:hi> which signifies no more than, <ns0:hi>O ye Christian men,</ns0:hi> as a <ns0:hi>sister,</ns0:hi> a <ns0:hi>wife</ns0:hi> signifies here a <ns0:hi>Christian wife.</ns0:hi> 6. That we no where read, that <ns0:hi>Peter, Iames, Iohn, Iudas</ns0:hi> (here called the Brethren of our Lord, or any of the other Apostles, ever in their travels car<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ried about with them any such rich matrons, not their wives, who (as those, <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> 8.3.) ministred to them of their sub<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stance. Our Interpreters have therefore justly translated it, a <ns0:hi>sister,</ns0:hi> a <ns0:hi>wife</ns0:hi>; and the sense is, Have I not power to marry? Yet the phrase teaches us two things: 1. That Christians have no power, that is, no lawful power to marry such as are no Christians, their wives must be their sisters also in Christ. 2. That <ns0:hi>husbands</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>wives</ns0:hi> ought to be undivided companions one to another.</ns0:note>, as well as other apostles, and <ns0:hi>as</ns0:hi> 
                  <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mark 6.3. Luke 6.16. Gal. 1.19.</ns0:note> the brethren of the Lord, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Matt. 8.1<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>
                  </ns0:note> and Cephas? <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">He instanceth in several Apostles that were marri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed, <ns0:hi>Peter</ns0:hi> (called <ns0:hi>Cephas,</ns0:hi>) <ns0:hi>Iames, Iohn,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Iudas</ns0:hi> the <ns0:hi>Son of Alpheus,</ns0:hi> Christs kinsmen. Whence we may observe, That Ministers may lawfully marry, no Law of God hath restrained them more than others: The Popish Doctrine forbidding to <ns0:hi>marry,</ns0:hi> is by the Apostle determined to be a Doctrine of Devils.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="6">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:445" />6 Or I onely, and Barnabas, <ns0:note place="margin">Thess. 3 9.</ns0:note> have not we pow<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />er to forbear working? <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Are I and <ns0:hi>Barnabas</ns0:hi> the alone Apostles, who are obliged for our livelihood to work with our hands? As <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> did, <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 18.3. making <ns0:hi>Tents.</ns0:hi> We certainly, as well as the rest of the Apostles, if we would run out to the utmost end of the line of our liberty in things, without having any regard to the circum<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stances of our brethren, might forbear working with our hands, and expect that those amongst whom we labour, should main<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tain us.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="7">7 Who <ns0:note place="margin">
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> Cor. 10.4.</ns0:note> goeth a warfare at any time at his own charges <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">The work of the Ministry is a warfare, the Ministers work in that Age was so in a more eminent manner, as the opposition which those first Ministers of the Gospel, both from the Jews, and from the Heathens, was greater than what Ministers have in later Ages met with. Now, saith the Apostle, none that lists an Army, expects that his Souldiers should maintain themselves without any pay.</ns0:note>? who <ns0:note place="margin">
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> 3.6, <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, 8.</ns0:note> planteth a vineyard, and eateth not of the fruit thereof <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">It is like the planting of a <ns0:hi>Vineyard.</ns0:hi> The Church in Scripture is called a Vineyard, <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 5.1, 2. The plants are the Lords, but he useth Ministers hands in the plant<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing of them; none planteth a vineyard, but in expectation of some fruit; none imployeth servants to plant a vineyard, but he resolveth to uphold them with food and raiment, while they are in his work.</ns0:note>? or who <ns0:note place="margin">
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>. 21.15. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>.2.</ns0:note> feed<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth a flock, and eateth not of the milk of the flock? <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">The Church is compared to a flock (saith the Apostle) no man feeds a flock either personally, or by his servants, but he eateth, or alloweth his servants to eat of the milk of the flock. By these three instances commonly known amongst men, the Apostle sheweth the reasonableness, that the Ministers of the Gospel should be maintained from the people, to whom they are Ministers.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="8">8 Say I these things as a man? or saith not the Law the same also? <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">That is, I do not speak this only rationally, or by a fallible Spirit, nor do I build this assertion alone upon instances known and familiar amongst men. As this is highly reasonable and conform to what the very light of Nature sheweth, and the Law of Nature obligeth men to in other cases where men take others off their own work, to attend theirs; so it is according to the Will of God, which is the highest reason.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="9">9 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> 
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>.12.</ns0:note> For it is written in the Law of Moses, Thou shalt not muzzle the mouth of the ox that treadeth out the corn <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Art being not so improved formerly as now, nor in all places as in some places; they were wont anciently both in the land of <ns0:hi>Iudea,</ns0:hi> and since in <ns0:hi>Greece,</ns0:hi> and (as is said) at this day in some places of <ns0:hi>France,</ns0:hi> to tread out their <ns0:hi>Corn</ns0:hi> by the <ns0:hi>feet of Oxen:</ns0:hi> and by the Law of <ns0:hi>Moses, Deut.</ns0:hi> 25.4. it should seem <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> some too covetous persons would muzzle the mouths of t<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                        <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>i<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> Oxen, that while they trod out the Corn, they might eat <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>o<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>e of it, which God looking upon as an act of cruelty or <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                        <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>mercifulness, forbad his ancient people the Jews.</ns0:note>: Doth God take care for oxen? <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Now, s<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ith the Apostle, <ns0:hi>doth God take care for oxen?</ns0:hi> that is, more for Oxen than for Ministers or Men? For God doth take care for o<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>e<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, he <ns0:hi>preserveth both man and beast</ns0:hi>; he takes care, as our S<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>vio<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>r elsewhere teacheth us, for the <ns0:hi>sparrows,</ns0:hi> for the <ns0:hi>fowls of t<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>e air,</ns0:hi> for the <ns0:hi>grass of the field,</ns0:hi> and therefore for <ns0:hi>Oxen,</ns0:hi> which are a degree of creatures more noble: but by the same reason we must conclude, That he taketh a greater care for men, espe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />c<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                        <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>lly such as he imployeth in his more immediate service.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="10">10 Or saith he it altogether for our sakes? For our sakes no doubt <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Not that the Law, <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 25.4. did primarily reveal Gods will for the maintenance of Ministers; for undoubtedly it did primarily oblige them according to the letter of it, not to deal cruelly and unmercifully with the beast they made use of, but as they took them off from getting their food, by taking them up to tread our corn for them; so while they did it, they should not <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                        <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>arve them, but give them leave moderately to eat of it. But (saith the Apostle) the reason of it doth much more oblige, with respect to men, especially such men as are imployed in a Ministry for your Souls.</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:hi>this</ns0:hi> is written, that <ns0:note place="margin">
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> 2.6.</ns0:note> he that ploweth, should plow in hope <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">That as he who ploweth for another, ploweth in hope to get bread for himself, from the wages for which he coven<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>n<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="3 letters">
                        <ns0:desc>•••</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>h.</ns0:note>, and he that thresh<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth in hope, should be partaker of his hope <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">And so also doth the thresher thresh in hope: So we <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>hat are the Lords Plow-men, working together with him (though in a far inferior degree of causation) in the plowing up the <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                        <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>llow grounds of mens hearts, and sowing the seed of righteousness in mens Souls, and the Lords <ns0:hi>Threshers,</ns0:hi> by our la<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bours, exhortations, arguments, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> beating the fruits of good <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                        <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>rks, to the glory of God, out of those amongst whom we labour, might also labour in some hope of a livelihood for our selves, while we are doing the Lords work and his peoples.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="11">11 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Rom. 15.27<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> Gal. 6.6.</ns0:note> If we have sown unto you spiritual things, <ns0:hi>is it</ns0:hi> a great thing if we shall reap your carnal things? <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">By spiritual things the Apostle meaneth the Doctrine and Sacraments of the Gospel, which are called spiritual things, be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause they come from Heaven, they affect the soul and spirit of a man, they tend to make men spiritual, they prepare the Soul for Heaven. By <ns0:hi>carnal things</ns0:hi> he means things which only serve our bodies, which are our carnal fleshly part. From the in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />equality of these things, and the excellency of the former above the latter, the Apostle argueth the reasonableness of Mi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nisters maintenance from their people, they giving them <ns0:hi>quid pro quo,</ns0:hi> a just compensation for such allowance, yea what was of much more value; for there is a great disproportion be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tween things spiritual and things carnal, the former much ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />celling the latter: so as the Minister of the Gospel had the odds of them, giving people things of a much greater and more ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cellent value, for things of a much lesser and inferior value.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="12">12 If others be partakers of <ns0:hi>this</ns0:hi> power over you, <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> not we rather <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Those false Apostles or Teachers, which were amongst the <ns0:hi>Corinthians,</ns0:hi> did (as it seemeth) exercise this power, that is, required maintenance of the people, saith the Apostle, Are not we by the same right possessed of such a power? Might not we as reasonably expect such a maintenance? <ns0:hi>Object.</ns0:hi> But might not they have said, No, you are not, they are constantly resi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ding amongst us, and instructing us? <ns0:hi>&c. Answ.</ns0:hi> This argu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing of the Apostle lets us know, that the Primitive Churches were not only obliged to maintain their own Pastors, but those also who were general Officers to the Church, and by the ap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pointment of God were not to fix and abide in any one place, but had the care of all the Churches upon them And it may also teach us, that though Christians be in the first place obli<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ged to take care of their own Pastors, yet they are not to limit their charity to them, but also to take what case their ability will allow them of others, whose labours have at any time been useful to them, or may be useful to any other part of the Church of God.</ns0:note>? <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Vers. 15. 2 Cor. 11.9. & 12.13.</ns0:note> Nevertheless, we have not used this power: but suffer all things, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">2 Cor. 11.12.</ns0:note> lest we should hinder the gospel of Christ <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Yet, saith the Apostle, though we have this pow<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />er or liberty, neither I nor <ns0:hi>Barnabas</ns0:hi> have made use of it, but suffer all those evils that come upon our not using it, <ns0:hi>hunger, thirst, labour,</ns0:hi> lest we should hinder the progress of the Gospel, while some might for the charge decline hearing us, or others might charge us with covetousness, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>

                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>eed.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> live <ns0:hi>of the things</ns0:hi> of the tem<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ple? and they which wait at the altar, are par<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />takers with the altar? <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">You may understand what is the mind and will of God under the New Testament, by reflecting upon what appeareth to you, to have been his mind and will under the Old Testa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment; God had a Ministry under the Old Testament, the <ns0:hi>Tribe of Levi</ns0:hi> was it, and God there ordained and appointed a liveli<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />hood for them, <ns0:hi>Num.</ns0:hi> 18.20. <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 10.9. & 18.1. so as they needed not (as other men) to labour with their hands to get bread to eat.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="14">14 Even so <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Matt. 10.10. Luke 10.7.</ns0:note> hath the Lord ordained <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Gods Will is the same under the New Testament that it was under the Old; it is not as to the people a matter of liber<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ty, so as men may chuse whether they will maintain their Mini<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sters or no, there is an Ordinance of God in the case: It is the Will of God, that those who are taken off from worldly imp<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>oy<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ments, and spend their <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ime in the study and preaching of the Gospel, should have a livelihood from their labour.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Gal. 6.6. 1 Tim. 5.17.</ns0:note> that they which preach the gospel, should live of the gospel.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="15">15 But <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Acts 18.3. Chap. 4.12. 1 Thess. 2.9. 2 Thess. 3.8.</ns0:note> I have used none of these things <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Though I have such a liberty to marry as well as others, and a liberty to demand a maintenance of those to whom I preach the Gospel, yet I have done neither.</ns0:note>. Neither have I written these things, that it should be <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                     <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                  </ns0:gap>o done unto me: for <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">2 Cor. 11.10.</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:hi>it were</ns0:hi> better for me to die, then that any man should make my glorying void <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Nor do I now write to that purpose, that I would now impose a burden upon you to raise me a maintenance. I know I am calumniated by some, as if by preaching the Gospel, I only sought my own pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fit and advantage, I have gloried in the contrary, <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 20.33. so <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 18. of this Chapter, and I look upon it as my great ho<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nour, that I can preach the Gospel freely, and I had rather die by starving, than lose this advantage of glorying. And if I for your profit, and for the advantage of the Gospel, abate of my liberty, should not you abate of yours, to keep your weak bre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thren from destroying their Souls by <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>inning against God?</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="16">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:446" />16 For though I preach the gospel, I have no<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thing to glory of <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Though I do preach the Gospel, yet<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> I have no reason at all to glory, all that I have to glory in, is, that I have preached it freely (which your false Apostles and Teachers do not) for the preaching of the Gospel, considered without that circum<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stance, I have no reason to glory in that, for I am in it but a Servant,</ns0:note>: <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Rom. 1.14.</ns0:note> for necessity is laid upon me, yea, wo is unto me, if I preach not the gospel <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">I am under the necessity of a Divine Precept to do that, and exposed to dreadful penalties and woes, if I do not do that; there is therefore no thanks I can claim upon that ac<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />count, all that I can glory in, is, that I do it without charge to those to whom I preach it. Some make a doubt, whether there lieth the same necessity upon Ministers now to preach the Go<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />spel, and they be liable to the same dangers and penalties, if they do it not. I see no reason at all to doubt it; for what necessity lay upon <ns0:hi>Paul,</ns0:hi> or any of the Apostles, but a necessity of Precept, that is, they were obliged to obey the Command of God in the case, and liable to such penalties in case of neg<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lect, as men are subject to, that obey not the Command of God, in fulfilling the duties of their Relations? The same ne<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cessity, the same danger is yet incumbent upon every Minister, or else we must say, That the Precepts commanding Ministers to preach, concerned the Apostles only, or that there is now no such Order of men as Ministers (both which are indeed said by <ns0:hi>Socinians</ns0:hi>
                     <ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>) If there be such an Ordinance of God as the Ministry, Ministers are under the Precepts given to Ministers, one of which is to <ns0:hi>preach</ns0:hi>; if they be under the same Precepts, there is the same necessity upon them of obeying them, that was upon <ns0:hi>Paul,</ns0:hi> and they are, in case of disobedience, subjected to the same <ns0:hi>Woes</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Penalties.</ns0:hi> Indeed every Minister is not bound to go up and down the World to preach, his relation is to a particular flock, that travelling to carry the Gospel about the World, was peculiar to the Apostles for the first plantation of the Gospel, but so was not preaching; if it had, <ns0:hi>Timothy</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Titus</ns0:hi> would have had no such charge as to that work. It is true, Ministers are not bound to preach in others houses with<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />out their leave; therefore we read very little of the Apostles preaching in the <ns0:hi>Temple</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Synagogues,</ns0:hi> nor without the leave of the Jews. But <ns0:hi>Paul, Acts</ns0:hi> 19.9. judged himself bound to preach in the School of <ns0:hi>Tyrannus,</ns0:hi> and in his own hired house at <ns0:hi>Rome, Acts</ns0:hi> 28.30, 31. For the circumstance of <ns0:hi>Numbers,</ns0:hi> to which they are bound to preach, the holy Scripture hath no where de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />termined, and Ministers are left to be guided by their own pru<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dence according to circumstances; but preach they must, if they be <ns0:hi>called of God,</ns0:hi> he hath sent them to it, fitted them for the work, and they have taken it upon them, and wo will be to every Minister, so called and sent of God, if he doth not fulfil his Ministry, as he hath opportunity and wisdom, consi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dering circumstances guideth him, in order to the end which he is to aim at, and to act for.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="17">17 For if I do this thing willingly, I have a re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ward <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">If I who have a liberty to take a maintenance for my labour in the Gospel, yet notwithstanding preach it freely, out of a free and chearful mind, desirous to promote the honour and glory of Christ, I then may expect a reward:</ns0:note>: but if against my will, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 4.1.</ns0:note> a dispensation <ns0:hi>of the gospel</ns0:hi> is committed to me <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">but if I only preach the Gospel, because there is a necessity laid upon me; all that can be said of me, is, that there is such a dispensation commit<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ted to me. The strength of the Apostles Argument seems to lie here, That no man can reasonably expect thanks, or any extra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ordinary reward for doing what he is obliged by his Superiors command under a great penalty to do. The Apostle was obliged by such a Precept, and under such penalties to preach the Go<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />spel; therefore he desired not only to do it, but to do it wil<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lingly and readily, a greater testimony of which could not be, than for him to do it, without desiring or expecting any reward for his pains, but what God of his free Grace should give him; this made this matter of glorifying to him, which he desired might not be in vain. So that though the word <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> here be truly tran<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />slated <ns0:hi>willingly,</ns0:hi> and opposed to <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, which is as truly translated <ns0:hi>unwillingly,</ns0:hi> yet it seems to comprehend <ns0:hi>without charge,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>taking nothing for his pains,</ns0:hi> as a demonstration of his willingness to, and chearful performance of his work, which being a thing as to which God had laid him under no necessity by any Precept, was matter of glorying to him against the false Apostles, who did otherwise, and also a ground for him to expect a greater reward from God, than those who, though they did the same work, yet did it not from the like free and chearful spirit.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="18">18 What is my reward then <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">What then is the ground of my expectation of a greater reward? Or wherein is the glorying I before mentioned? Not in the performance of the work, for as to that I am under a ne<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cessity to do it, and under a penalty, if I neglect it:</ns0:note>? Verily, that when I preach the gospel, I may make the gospel of Christ without charge <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">but it lieth here, that when I preach the Gospel, I do it freely, and make it without charge; a thing, which as to the substance of the work, he was not by any Law of God bound to do, yet was not this in <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> a work of Supererogation; for circumstances might so rule, and (doubtless <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> apprehended they did so) that it might be his duty so to do. For though the Minister may law<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fully take maintenance from the people, where he cannot sup<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />port himself without their assistance; yet if the case be such, that he can subsist without it, and the people be so poor, that they are not able to give it; or if he seeth it will hinder the Gospel, keeping many from coming within the sound of what must be chargeable to them, and open the mouths of Enemies; it is matter of duty to him, under such circumstan<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ces, to preach freely. Though considering the thing in it self separately from such circumstances, the Minister may lawfully enough require and expect such maintenance.</ns0:note>, that I abuse not my power in the gospel <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">That (saith the Apostle) I abuse not my power in the Gospel. Some think that the word here translated <ns0:hi>abuse,</ns0:hi> might better have been translated <ns0:hi>use,</ns0:hi> as it signified <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 7.31. But it generally sig<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nifies abuse, so as there is no reason to vary from the common usage of it, according to which it teaches us this remarkable Lesson, That so to use a liberty which God hath left us as to actions, as that by our use of it the Glory of God, or the good of others is hindred, is to abuse it, that is, not to use it to that true end for which God hath betrusted us with it. For this is certain, that God hath betrusted us with no power or liberty to be used to the prejudice of his Glory, which is the great end of our lives, or to the prejudice of the spiritual good and ad<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vantage of others. All such use of our liberty in any thing, is indeed an abuse of it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="19">19 For though I be free from all men <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">The word <ns0:hi>men</ns0:hi> is not in the <ns0:hi>Greek,</ns0:hi> but is supplied by our Interpreters. Some make <ns0:hi>things</ns0:hi> the Substantive, and restrain it to the things of the Ceremonial Law, it may be understood both of <ns0:hi>men</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>things</ns0:hi>; he was born no mans servant, nor by Gods Law made a servant to any mens humors, and as free, as to many other things, as he was to have taken maintenance of the Churches, for the pains he bestowed amongst them.</ns0:note>, yet have I made my self servant unto all, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Matt. 18.1<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>. 1 Pet. 3.1.</ns0:note> that I might gain the more <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Yet (saith he) observe my practice, that I might gain men to Christ (so the Apostle several times calleth converting Souls, bringing them in love with the Gospel, and into a road that may bring them to Heaven, which we ought to account the greatest gain in the world, as it appeareth from <ns0:hi>Dan.</ns0:hi> 12.3.) I have become, or made my self, the <ns0:hi>Servant of all,</ns0:hi> not the Servant of their lusts and corruptions (that is the way to lose mens Souls, and destroy them, not to gain them) but a Ser<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vant to their <ns0:hi>weaknesses</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>infirmities</ns0:hi> so far, as they were not sinful: I have denied my self in my liberty, and determined my self to that part in my actions, which I saw would most ob<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lige, profit, and indear them to me, and to bring them more in love with the Gospel.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="20">20 And <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Acts 1<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>.1<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>
                  </ns0:note> unto the Jews I became as a Jew <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">The Ceremonial Law died with Christ, <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 2.15, 16. wherefore Christians were not obliged to the performance and observation of it after the death of Christ; but it pleased God for a time to indulge the Jews the observance of those Rites, until they could clearly see, and be fully perswaded of their li<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />berty from it, with which Christ had made them free, and it was some good time before all those, who from Judaism had turned to Christianity, could be thus perswaded, as we may learn from <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 4.21. they <ns0:hi>desired to be under the Law.</ns0:hi> To such (saith the Apostle) <ns0:hi>I became as a Iew,</ns0:hi> that is, I observed some Rites, which the Ceremonial Law (peculiar to the Jews) re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />quired; an instance of which we have <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 21.23, 24. where we find <ns0:hi>Paul purifying himself</ns0:hi> (according to the Rites of the Ceremonial Law) with <ns0:hi>four men which had a vow upon them.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>, that I might gain the Jews: to them that are un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />der the Law, as under the Law, that I might gain them that are under the Law <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">The Jews before Christs death were under the Law; many of them, though converted to the Christian Religion after the death of Christ, apprehended themselves under the Law, not as yet seeing the liberty with which Christ had made them <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ree (saith the Apostle) I knowing the Will of God, for a time that the Jews should be indulged as to their weakness, became as one of them under the Law; <ns0:hi>that I might gain them,</ns0:hi> that is, reconcile them to the Christian Religion, and in some measure prepare them for receiving the Gospel. We have an instance of this in <ns0:hi>Pauls</ns0:hi> practice, <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 16.3. where he circumcised <ns0:hi>Timothy,</ns0:hi> because his mother was a <ns0:hi>Iew,</ns0:hi> that he might not irritate the Jews in those quarters, nor estrange them from the Doctrine of the Gospel. In all this <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> did nothing that was sinful, but only determined himself as to the liberty which God had given him, when he might <ns0:hi>do</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>forbea<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>,</ns0:hi> either doing or forbearing to do, as he saw the one or the other, made most for the honour and glory of God in the winning of Souls.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="21">21 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Gal. 2.<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>
                  </ns0:note> To them that are without Law, as with<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />out Law <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">It is manifest by the opposition of <ns0:hi>those that are without Law,</ns0:hi> mentioned in this verse, to <ns0:hi>those under the Law,</ns0:hi> mention<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed in the former verse, that as by the latter the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> are under<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stood, so by the former the <ns0:hi>Gentiles</ns0:hi> are to be understood, who were under no obligation to the observance either of the <ns0:hi>Cere<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />monial,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Iudicial Law,</ns0:hi> given to the <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ews; the one to guide that Nation in the matters of Worship till Christ should come; the other to guide them in matters of Civil Justice, as well as in Criminal causes, as matters of Plea and Trespass; <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>o that the term <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> here <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ignifieth differently from what it signifieth in many other Scriptures; where it signifieth men that live as they list, without any regard to any Laws of God or men, as <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> 15.28. <ns0:hi>Luke.</ns0:hi> 22.37. <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 2.23. 2 <ns0:hi>Thess.</ns0:hi> 2.8. 1 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 1.9, &c.</ns0:note>, (<ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> being not without Law to God, but under the Law to Christ) that I might gain them that are without Law <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">This the Apostle makes appear by the next words, where he tells us, he was not <ns0:hi>without Law to God,</ns0:hi> but <ns0:hi>under the Law to Christ,</ns0:hi> though to the <ns0:hi>Gentiles</ns0:hi> he behaved himself, as if he him<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />self had been a <ns0:hi>Gentile,</ns0:hi> that is, forbearing the observances of the <ns0:hi>Levitical Law,</ns0:hi> to which the Gentiles had never any obliga<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion at all, yet he did not behave himself as one that had no regard to the Law of God, that was yet in force and obligato<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ry, but acknowledged himself to be under that, though a Ser<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vant of Christ's: so that he abated nothing of his necessary du<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ty, only denied himself in some things as to which the Law of God had left him a liberty, both to the Jews and Gentiles, pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pounding to himself the same end as to both, that is, the gain<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing of their Souls to Christ.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="22">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:446" />22 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> 13.1. 1 Cor. 11.29.</ns0:note> To the weak became I as weak, that I might gain the weak <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">To those that I observed weak in knowledge and Faith, who had not such a firm perswasion of the lawfulness of some things (suppose Circumcision, Purifyings required by the Law of <ns0:hi>Moses,</ns0:hi> &c.) <ns0:hi>I became as weak,</ns0:hi> that is, I yielded to them, and the things being to me matters of liberty, whcih I knew I might do, or not do, and be no transgressor of Gods Law, they not being able to comply with me, I complied with them, aba<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ting my liberty to gratifie their Consciences, though I knew that it was weakness in them, yet I indulged it, and made my more knowledge serve them in their weakness, so that I might not lose them.</ns0:note>: I <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Cap. 10.33.</ns0:note> am made all things to all men, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> 11.14. C<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                        <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>p. 7.16.</ns0:note> that I might by all means save some <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Thus, that I might be an instrument in any de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gree to save them, according to the various perswasions of se<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />veral Christians, I behaved my self towards them, doing nothing to gratifie them, by doing of which I knew, or had the least jealousie I should offend God, but not refusing any thing, ei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther as to doing or forbearing (which by the Law of God I saw I might do or forbear) where I saw the least hopes, by such do<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing or forbearing, to do the Souls of those good, in order to their eternal Salvation, with whom I was, and for whose sake I so did, or forbare any thing. O the humility and charity of this great Apostle! What an Example hath he set to all? (for none can pretend to a greater Superiority over men, as to spi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ritual things, than he unquestionably had.)</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="23">23 And this I do for the gospels sake <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> had two great ends, which he aimed at, in this de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nial of himself in these points of liberty; the one was the do<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="3 letters">
                        <ns0:desc>•••</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> good to the Souls both of Jews and Gentiles, this he had before instanced in: the other was the <ns0:hi>glory of God,</ns0:hi> which is that which he here meaneth by this phrase, <ns0:hi>for the Gospels sake,</ns0:hi> which he before expounded <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 12. lest <ns0:hi>we should hinder the Go<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />spel of Christ.</ns0:hi> By <ns0:hi>Pauls</ns0:hi> tenacious adhering to one part in a thing wherein he had liberty, <ns0:hi>the Gospel,</ns0:hi> that is, the progress or success of the Gospel, might have been hindred, both by the <ns0:hi>reproaches of Enemies,</ns0:hi> and also by the <ns0:hi>alienation</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>estrange<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment</ns0:hi> of the hearts of weaker Christians, or laying stumbling-blocks before them, at which they might fall, being imbolden<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed by the examples of their Guides, to do what (though law<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ful in it self) yet they judged unlawful.</ns0:note>, that I might be partaker thereof with <ns0:hi>you</ns0:hi> 
                  <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">I did it (saith he) that I might bring you into the <ns0:hi>fellowship</ns0:hi> of the Gospel, I had rather <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>o interpret it, than of the <ns0:hi>reward</ns0:hi> of the Gospel (as it pleaseth some.) The humility of the great Apostle is very re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />markable; he disdaineth not to be <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, a partaker in the Gospel with the meanest Members of the Church; he is not ashamed to call those Brethren whom his <ns0:hi>Lord</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Master</ns0:hi> is not ashamed so to call.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="24">24 Know ye not that they which run in a race, run all, but one receiveth the prize <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">The Apostle presseth all his former discourse by minding them of the difficulty of getting to Heaven, and of the obliga<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion that lay upon them to be the first in the spiritual Race. To this purpose he fetcheth a similitude from what they saw daily in the practice of those who frequented those Games by which the <ns0:hi>Romans</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Corinthians</ns0:hi> were wont to divert themselves. They had several, known by the names of the <ns0:hi>Olympian, Pythian, Nemean,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Isthmian Games,</ns0:hi> the latter of which were most proper to <ns0:hi>Greece.</ns0:hi> At these Games there were several that ran Races, either on foot, or on horse-back; and several that wrest<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />led, the Reward was a <ns0:hi>Crown</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Garland:</ns0:hi> and for those that ran, we read that the Crown or Garland was hung up at the end of the Race, and those who running on foot or on horse<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />back, could first lay hold upon it, and take it down, had it, so as though many ran, yet but one had the Crown: So, he saith, it is as to getting to Heaven; men might think it was a light matter, but they who would have the Crown of Glory must run for it, and it was a work required so much striving and labour, that not many would have that Crown; which is the same with that which our Saviour saith, <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> 13.24. <ns0:hi>For many shall seek to entes in, and shall not enter.</ns0:hi> 2 Tim. 2.5. <ns0:hi>If a man strive for masteries, he is not crowned, except he strive lawfully.</ns0:hi>

                     </ns0:gap>.1.</ns0:note> So run that ye may obtain <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Therefore (saith the Apostle) make it your business <ns0:hi>so to run, that you may ob<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tain,</ns0:hi> not only to do things in themselves lawful or good, but which are so cloathed with all their circumstances, and in the best manner for the glory of God, and the good of others.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="25">25 And every man that <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Eph. 6.12. 1 Tim. 6.12. 2 Tim. 2.5. & 4.7.</ns0:note> striveth for the ma<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stery <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">This is not all that is required of men that would go to Heaven, that they do not make an ill use of their liberty, using it to the dishonour of God, or to the prejudice of others; but look as it is with Wrestlers in those Games, in practice amongst you, they are <ns0:hi>temperate in all things,</ns0:hi> in the use of meats and drinks, or any pleasures, though in themselves lawful, they will so use them, as may best serve their end<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> upholding the strength of their body for the motion they are to use, and yet not clog<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ging them, or so using them, that they shall indispose them to, or hinder them in that motion which they are to use.</ns0:note>, is temperate in all things <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">We that are Christians, and striving for Heaven, should also do the like, so behaving our selves in the use of meats, drinks, appa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rel, pleasures, as the things so used by us, may serve us in our business for Heaven, and be no clog or hindrance to us.</ns0:note>: Now they <ns0:hi>do it</ns0:hi> to obtain a corruptible crown, but we an <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">2 Tim. 4.8. Jam. 1.12. 1 Pet. 5.4. Rev. 2.10. & 3.11.</ns0:note> incorruptible <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">And we have reason so to do, or we shall be shamed by those Gamesters; for they in that manner deny, restrain, and go<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vern themselves to get a Crown, which when they have, is a pitiful, corruptible, perishing thing; we do it for a Crown that is <ns0:hi>incorruptible; An inheritance incorruptible, and undefiled, that <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>adeth not away, reserved in heaven for us,</ns0:hi> as the Apostle speak<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth, 1 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 1.4.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="26">26 I therefore so run, not as uncertainly: so fight I, not as one that beateth the air <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">The Apostle proposeth his own example, As it is obser<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ved in Country-work, he that only bids his Servants do work, and puts not his own hand to it, or at least doth not attend and overlook them in their work, hath little done: So it is as obser<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vable in spiritual work, that a Minister of the Gospel, who, only in the Pulpit, dictates duty to others; but, out of it, doth no<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thing of it himself, seldom doth any good by his preaching. People not naturally inclined to any spiritual duty, have the old Proverb, <ns0:hi>Physician, cure thy self,</ns0:hi> at their tongues end, and are hard to believe that Teacher, who doth not in some mea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sure live up to his own Doctrine. Therefore, saith the Apo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stle, <ns0:hi>I run,</ns0:hi> I am in the same Race with you, and running to the same mark and for the same <ns0:hi>prize.</ns0:hi> I give you no other counsel than I my self take, I endeavour so to live, so in all things to behave my self, as I may not be at uncertainties whe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther I please God by my actions, or shall get to Heaven yea or no. I am a Fellow-Souldier with you, fighting against sin, I make it my great business not so to fight, so to resist sin, as if I did <ns0:hi>beat the air,</ns0:hi> that is, get no more fruit, profit, or ad<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vantage by it, than if I threw stones against the wind, or with a staff did beat the air. It is not every running, or every fight<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing, that will bring a man to Heaven, it must be a running with all our might, and continuing our motion till we come to the end of our Race, a fighting with all our might, and that against all sin.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="27">27 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Rom. 8.13.</ns0:note> But I keep under my body, and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Rom. 6.18, 19.</ns0:note> bring it into subjection <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Here the Apostle informs us how he ran, that he might not run uncertainly; how he fought, so as he might not be like one beating the air: <ns0:hi>I</ns0:hi> (saith he) <ns0:hi>keep under my body, and bring it into subjection.</ns0:hi> By <ns0:hi>Body</ns0:hi> here, we must not under<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stand only the Apostles fleshly part (which we usually call our body) no nor only our more gross and filthy affections and lusts (as some of the Schoolmen have thought) but what the Apostle elsewhere calleth the <ns0:hi>Old man,</ns0:hi> under which notion co<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />meth the sinful inclinations of our will, and corrupt dictates of Reason, as it is in man since the Fall. All this, as it cometh un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />der the notion of the flesh in many other places of Scripture, and of our <ns0:hi>members which are upon the earth,</ns0:hi> Col. 3.5. So it cometh here under the notion of <ns0:hi>the body</ns0:hi>; and indeed is that which our Apostle calleth, <ns0:hi>The body of death,</ns0:hi> Rom. 7.24. This was the object of the <ns0:hi>Apostles</ns0:hi> action. The object about which he was exercised. For his <ns0:hi>action,</ns0:hi> or exercise about this ob<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ject, is expressed by two words, <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> and <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> the former word (as some think) is borrowed from the pra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ctice of those that fought in the afore-mentioned Games, who knockt and beat one another till they were black and blue, and forced to yield themselves conquered. The second word sig<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nifieth to make one a Servant, to bring one under command, so as he will do what another would have him do. By these two words the Apostle expresseth, that <ns0:hi>Mortification,</ns0:hi> which he de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />clareth himself to have lived in the practice of, that he might not in his Race for Heaven run incertainly, nor in his spiritual fight lose his labour, and reap no more profit, than one should reap that spends his time in beating the air. Their sense who think that this duty of <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> was discharged by acts of meer ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ternal discipline, such as fasting, wearing sackcloth, beating themselves, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> is much too short; these things reach not to the mind of man, his corrupt affections and lusts which give life to the extravagancy of the bodily members, though indeed they may some of them be good means in order to the greater work. <ns0:hi>Pauls</ns0:hi> meaning was, that he made it his work to deny his sensi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tive appetite such gratifyings as it would have to resist the ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />travagant motions of his will, yea of his own corrupt reason, so far as they were in any thing contrary to the holy Will of God; though in order to this, he also used Fasting and Prayer, and such acts of external Discipline, as his wisdom taught him, were any way proper to this end: And this he tells us that he did,</ns0:note>: lest that by any means, when I have preached to others, I my self should be a cast-away <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>lest while he preached to others, he himself should be a cast-away.</ns0:hi> From whence we may observe, That <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> thought such a thing possible, that one who all his life had been preaching to others, to bring them to Heaven, might himself be thrown into Hell at last; and if it had not, our Saviour would never have told us, That he would at the last day say to some, <ns0:hi>Depart from me, I know you not, you workers of iniquity:</ns0:hi> who for their admittance had pleaded, <ns0:hi>We have prophesied in thy Name.</ns0:hi> Nor must we que<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stion but <ns0:hi>Iudas</ns0:hi> whom our Saviour calls a <ns0:hi>Son of perdition,</ns0:hi> was a lost man as to Eternity, though it be certain, that he as well as the other Apostles, was a Preacher of the Gospel: yea, so f<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>r is this from being impossible, that it was the opinion of <ns0:hi>Chrysostom,</ns0:hi> That few Ministers would be saved. We may also further observe, That such Ministers as indulge their body, gi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ving themselves liberties, either more externally in meats, drinks, apparel, pleasures; or more internally, indulging themselves in sinful speculations, motions, affections, inclinations, take a quite contrary road to Heaven than <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> took; and think they have a great deal more liberty to the flesh than S. <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> thought he had, or than he durst use.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
